comments.text:
I'm confused. What is the best practice now for controlling the variable traditionally referred to as "race"/"ethnic groups"? 

Quotes from the paper above:

"The National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) issued a report providing recommendations on using race, ethnicity, ancestry, and other descriptors of population stratification (112). The NASEM report asserts that race does not have any biological basis and emphasizes that researchers not use continental labels (that is, African, European, Asian, Native American, and Oceanian ancestry) or socially constructed racial and ethnic categories in genetics studies (Asian, Black, white, etc.). Similarly, for neuroimaging studies, researchers should not blindly “control for race” in brain-based association studies with nonbrain variables, especially when race and ethnicity are patterned onto said variables (113–115). We acknowledge the complicated historical and present social and economic backdrop in which race, ethnicity, and SES co-occur.

The current study follows these NASEM recommendations and therefore does not evaluate race and ethnicity as target variables in univariate and multivariate brain association models (116, 117). Genetic ancestry is defined within the context of genetic admixture of specific, idiosyncratic reference populations (in this case, ABCD). Ancestral inference methods [principal components analysis (PCA) in ABCD], although more robust than self-reported race, can still be biased by the sampling process and model parameters (118). The UK Biobank is more homogeneous than the ABCD Study with respect to race (95% white British, white Irish, or other white background), therefore it was used for control analyses, which showed that the results held in this type of sample (fig. S7)."

items.title: Patterns of brain-wide associations reflect socioeconomics
items.abstract: Previous brain-wide association studies (BWAS) have linked specific environmental and behavioral variables to brain variability. In this work, we mapped 649 variables to children’s brains and compared the resultant BWAS maps with each other and with neurobiological reference patterns. Socioeconomic status (SES) showed the strongest brain-wide associations. The SES associations were strongest in motor and sensory but not cognitive regions, a pattern shared across many BWAS maps, including intelligence quotient (IQ). A single, common BWAS brain pattern existed across variables that was most reflective of a child’s socioeconomics. Adjusting for SES weakened brain-IQ associations, eliminating the BWAS motor and sensory pattern. Brain-with-IQ associations also did not generalize when trained on higher-SES subsamples. Thus, children’s brains vary the most with SES, potentially through SES-dependent sleep deprivation and stress.
items.summary: Analyzed brain-wide association studies across 649 variables in children and found socioeconomic status showed the strongest and most generalizable brain associations, largely explaining brain-IQ links.
items.key_finding: A single common brain pattern linked to socioeconomic status underlay many brain-wide associations including IQ, and adjusting for SES eliminated the motor/sensory BWAS pattern for IQ.

classification.notes: Only abstract available; approach tags inferred from BWAS methodology typical of large consortium mega-analyses.

It's about growing work on AI homogeneity, even across models. 
https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22954 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.22954)

I personally don't think homogenizing thinking is a good thing. And also that AI may not be as creative as one would believe.

This is a summary at end of the blog post (by an LLM, which adds an unnecessary 3rd point I'm leaving off):
1. Here is a mechanism (statistical attractors formed from contaminated/uncurated training data, reinforced through feedback loops)
2. Here is proof the mechanism works (Elara, documented across 13 providers, persistent across generations)
Is our general satisfaction with its coding abilities reflective of our own lack of coding creativity or expectations thereof?

@member Yeah, it's just a curious but inevitable phenomenon, but I don't fully understand precisely how different models are led to such a small convergent solution.
@member Fair point, but I do think there is not much incentive for a coding solution to be creative, rather than functional. Which might even be anti-correlated with creativity (tried and tested things are known to work).

I mean, we see representational convergence in toy models with matched architecture and training data. It's well established. I've spent years now talking about this, and I think this is basically the only thing I talked about in my last lab meeting presentation. In that time there's been an active debate in the CS community regarding whether there's cross-architectural convergence as well, and it serves as the basis for multimodal model stitching. This convergence you're citing @member is very granular, but seems consistent with that model. All those focus on representations, but there's a tight coupling in ANNs between representations and behavior. But if this is in fact what you're talking about, then there are much better examples from the CS research community than these naive user experiences exemplified here. I especially like Kornblith 2019 ArXiv and Saxe 2019 PNAS. But Huh 2024 ArXiv (https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2405.07987) might be more relevant here.
Elara,  _Elara, or Elara_ don't seem very token efficient.
@member Good point - but I think latent representation convergence is necessary but not sufficient for model output convergence?
You can still generate different model outputs from two models with similar-ish latent representations?
your outputs can't be more different than your representations in a feedforward network
the representations establish the upper bound
the discrepancy arises from the dimensionality reduction that happens at the output layer

I've been bandying about this figure to show representational convergence. It breaks down the underlying topographic resnet-18 networks into marr's levels. Activations are the implementation level, representations are the algorithmic level, and the prediction are the function. You can see right there in the top two pannels how representational convergence leads to functional convergence. Panel C also (somewhat indirectly) shows how networks that have more similar representations (non-topographic ResNets) also have more similar function (predictions, "model agreement") than networks with more idiosyncratic representations (TDANNs, the topographic resnets).

We gotta talk more I guess. Correct me if I am wrong - but isn't the fact that you are obtaining different topographies from same geometries exactly my point that you can get different model outputs from the same representation?

See this toy example: you have the same latent representation (z) for two binary classifiers. But for model 1 the output layer has class = 1 iff z>0; and for model 2, class = 1 iff z<0. Now the models disagree 100% of the time despite the same internal representation?

no, it's not the same point at all. The point of this figure is to demonstrate that implementations can be degenerate, not that function is degenerate. implementation -> representation -> function. The variable topographeis is on the other side of representational convergence from function.

the toy example is wrong. If you have two models and one is z > 0 -> class 1 and the other has z < 0 -> class 1 then your readout layer is either categorically wrong in one case, and categorically correct in the other or a mixture of nonsense. That readout layer's representations (the readout layer, post layer z) are then no longer equivalent, and that scenario is also unlikely to ever be obtained except if hand coded.
for representational convergence with different behavior you would need to introduce some intermediate representational divergence between readout and whatever layre you idetnify as convergent
claiming representations -> function in that sense is borderline tautological in a feedforward network.

you can imagine a scenario though with multiple parallel streams (e.g. alexnet has two independent streams one trained on one GPU and one trained on a different GPU), in which case you can have convergence on one stream but not the other and divergence in function due to the contribution of the divergent stream.

this is the scenario faced by the brain, where the network topology is not linear, but rather has multiple branches, so a representation in one area is not necessarily tethered to behavior and you need to intervene to perturb the representation and observe a perturbation of behavior to demonstrate that representation is actually used.

Ah, I see, your topographies are not the model output, fair point. But regarding the divergence from common latent space, it is still possible naturalistically. But I do agree that it probably needs more than one layer. Example I am thinking of are autoencoder type networks where you can freeze the encoder to create a shared latent space, but you can basically construct any kind of decoder on top of it.

I am still going to stand by "latent representation convergence is necessary but not sufficient for model output convergence" but I can see why you'd think otherwise, especially in strict feed forward nets.

I don’t get it. You’re just moving the goalpost. Your decoder introduced a new representation that you’re deliberately choosing to be different. You don’t get to claim you have different outputs from similar representations when you do that. The representations cease being similar exactly at the point that causes the outputs to differ.

Well, we did start this thread talking about LLMs after all which do have a separate decoder element (albeit a very simple one), but you can just freeze the encoder element (i.e. transformer part) and extract different outputs from decoders. Anyway, discuss more in person I guess.

items.title: Artificial Hivemind: The Open-Ended Homogeneity of Language Models (and Beyond)
items.abstract: Language models (LMs) often struggle to generate diverse, human-like creative content, raising concerns about the long-term homogenization of human thought through repeated exposure to similar outputs. Yet scalable methods for evaluating LM output diversity remain limited, especially beyond narrow tasks such as random number or name generation, or beyond repeated sampling from a single model. We introduce Infinity-Chat, a large-scale dataset of 26K diverse, real-world, open-ended user queries that admit a wide range of plausible answers with no single ground truth. We introduce the first comprehensive taxonomy for characterizing the full spectrum of open-ended prompts posed to LMs, comprising 6 top-level categories (e.g., brainstorm & ideation) that further breaks down to 17 subcategories. Using Infinity-Chat, we present a large-scale study of mode collapse in LMs, revealing a pronounced Artificial Hivemind effect in open-ended generation of LMs, characterized by (1) intra-model repetition, where a single model consistently generates similar responses, and more so (2) inter-model homogeneity, where different models produce strikingly similar outputs. Infinity-Chat also includes 31,250 human annotations, across absolute ratings and pairwise preferences, with 25 independent human annotations per example. This enables studying collective and individual-specific human preferences in response to open-ended queries. Our findings show that LMs, reward models, and LM judges are less well calibrated to human ratings on model generations that elicit differing idiosyncratic annotator preferences, despite maintaining comparable overall quality. Overall, INFINITY-CHAT presents the first large-scale resource for systematically studying real-world open-ended queries to LMs, revealing critical insights to guide future research for mitigating long-term AI safety risks posed by the Artificial Hivemind.
items.summary: The authors introduced Infinity-Chat, a large dataset of open-ended human queries and human annotations, to study mode collapse and homogeneity in language model outputs, termed the 'Artificial Hivemind' effect.
items.key_finding: Language models exhibit both intra-model repetition and inter-model homogeneity in open-ended generation, and are poorly calibrated to human ratings on prompts eliciting idiosyncratic preferences.

items.title: Cerebellar Transcranial Alternating Current Stimulation in the Theta Band Prevents Recall of the Initial Fear Association After Extinction Training
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Although the neural network underlying fear extinction has been extensively studied, the cerebellum's role has received little attention – despite its well‐established involvement in associative learning. Our study therefore aimed to provide additional evidence that the cerebellum is part of the circuitry supporting fear‐extinction processes, and to get a better understanding of how the cerebellum may contribute to fear extinction learning. In this study, 6 Hz cerebellar transcranial alternating current stimulation (ctACS) or sham stimulation was applied during extinction training in a two‐day differential fear conditioning paradigm in young, healthy participants undergoing 3T fMRI, using a double‐blind randomized design. Acquisition and extinction training occurred on day 1, followed by extinction recall on day 2. Skin conductance responses showed that 6 Hz ctACS applied during extinction training reduced spontaneous fear recovery during recall. During extinction training, differential fMRI activation (CS+ > CS‐) was significantly higher in the occipital cortex in the verum compared to the sham group. During recall, differential fMRI activation was significantly higher in the precentral gyrus in the sham compared to the verum group at the time the aversive unconditioned response (US) was expected but did not occur. Furthermore, in recall, parametric modulation based on trial‐by‐trial model‐derived prediction errors for no‐US events revealed significantly higher activation in frontal cortical areas, including the anterior cingulate cortex, and parietal cortical areas in the sham compared to the verum group. Volume of interest analyses showed significantly higher beta values towards the CS+ compared to the CS‐ in the sham group, but not in the verum group in the right insula related to the prediction of the US and its unexpected omission in early recall. Although direct stimulation effects cannot be ruled out, 6 Hz ctACS‐related increases in activation in visual regions during extinction training may indicate enhanced attention to CS‐related visual and/or contextual cues. Furthermore, 6 Hz ctACS facilitated the downregulation of brain regions involved in fear conditioning during recall, potentially reducing spontaneous recovery. Future studies are warranted to further evaluate whether enhancement of cerebellar theta oscillations can help to stabilize extinction effects and therefore support exposure therapy.

items.message:
Genealogical link (in the Nietzschian/Foucaultian sense of the lineage of an idea) between Wittgenstein and modern LLMs:

“Margaret Masterman was a student [(one of six)] in Wittgenstein’s 1933-1934 course, the lecture notes of which were collected in the “Blue Book”. The ideas in that course were the foundational ones later contained in the “Philosophical Investigations”: the specific insight that the meaning of words derives from their use in language constituted the basis of Masterman’s computational approach to linguistics -focused on meaning and thesauri rather than syntax -, which she applied in particular to machine translation. She founded the Cambridge Language Research Unit in 1955, and work coming from there influenced researchers all around the world for the following decades, in a time when Chomskian ideas [Cho57] were predominant (Sixties) and Montague proposed his logic-based theories [Mon74] (early Seventies).”

https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01570 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.01570)

Personally I suspect a link between the tractatus and latent semantic analysis on the one hand and philosophical investigations and next token prediction on the other. This author advances a different take and neglects the tractatus entirely. But I thought the direct link drawn via this student was an interesting bit of historical trivia that makes the otherwise vibe based impression I’ve got of a link more plausible. Maybe someone else might enjoy this too.

Vagus nerve stimulation for analgesia and a brainstem based pathway:
https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-026-02313-0 (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-026-02313-0)
items.title: A brainstem pathway underlying vagal modulation of somatic pain and affective states
items.abstract: Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) alleviates pain, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain elusive. Furthermore, the caudal nucleus of the solitary tract (cNTS) receives vagal and somatic inputs, but how it transforms pain signals into behavior and how VNS modulates this processing remain unclear. Here we identified a population of cNTS neurons projecting to the periaqueductal gray (PAG) (cNTSPAG) as a critical node for VNS-dependent suppression of pain and negative affect in mice. Optogenetic activation of cNTSPAG neurons recapitulated pain behavior. These neurons exhibited modality-specific encoding of pain and predictive signals after learning. Inhibition of spinal input-defined cNTSPAG neurons reduced mechanical, but not thermal, nociception. Notably, VNS selectively dampened pain-evoked cNTSPAG activity by recruiting local inhibition and attenuated pain-evoked dopamine reductions in the nucleus accumbens through cNTSPAG. Our findings establish a brainstem pathway with a previously unrecognized role in VNS modulation of pain and negative affect, providing insights for targeted neuromodulation in pain management. This study identifies a brainstem pathway through which vagus nerve stimulation reduces pain and negative affect, showing how the caudal nucleus of the solitary tract transforms pain signals and regulates pain-related dopamine responses.
items.summary: Researchers identified a brainstem pathway from the caudal nucleus of the solitary tract to the periaqueductal gray that mediates vagus nerve stimulation's suppression of pain and negative affect in mice.
items.key_finding: cNTS neurons projecting to PAG (cNTSPAG) encode pain modality-specifically, and VNS dampens their pain-evoked activity via local inhibition, attenuating pain-related dopamine reductions in the nucleus accumbens.

classification.notes: Animal (mouse) study using optogenetics and circuit tracing rather than fMRI; approach tags reflect brain_stimulation (VNS/optogenetics) though not human neuroimaging methods per se.

comments.text:
Also, other very well-known but seemingly problematic findings:
https://x.com/salonium/status/2042941845437583377

Interesting. I've taken Park et al 2023 to heart maybe more than is good for me. If the disruptiveness of publications and patents is not in fact going down, and the siloing of disciplines is historically typical, or increasing without consequence, both would be major updates to my mental models of meta-science. Feels like the siloing in particular has been a consistent thorn in my side for at least a decade and I'm not very inclined to tolerate it as a mundane and inconsequential reality of science.

The gist seems to be that a bunch of papers with citations were indexed in the citation database as making no references (paradigm shifting papers have a tendency to make few citations, see Einstein "On The Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies" 1905 Annalen der Physik: 5 citations, or Watson and Crick "Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids" 1953 Nature: 6 citations), but in fact did make references. It's weird that this would systematically bias findings though. It reads as a parsing error that shouldn't be correlated with scientific disruption?

Although, I guess if it's an OCR error, it would be more common in the past when things were not typeset as consistently, or fully digitized as they are today, and thus covary with the dependent variable of interest (time)...

items.title: Dataset Artefacts are the Hidden Drivers of the Declining Disruptiveness in Science
items.abstract: Park et al. [1] reported a decline in the disruptiveness of scientific and technological knowledge over time. Their main finding is based on the computation of CD indices, a measure of disruption in citation networks [2], across almost 45 million papers and 3.9 million patents. Due to a factual plotting mistake, database entries with zero references were omitted in the CD index distributions, hiding a large number of outliers with a maximum CD index of one, while keeping them in the analysis [1]. Our reanalysis shows that the reported decline in disruptiveness can be attributed to a relative decline of these database entries with zero references. Notably, this was not caught by the robustness checks included in the manuscript. The regression adjustment fails to control for the hidden outliers as they correspond to a discontinuity in the CD index. Proper evaluation of the Monte-Carlo simulations reveals that, because of the preservation of the hidden outliers, even random citation behaviour replicates the observed decline in disruptiveness. Finally, while these papers and patents with supposedly zero references are the hidden drivers of the reported decline, their source documents predominantly do make references, exposing them as pure dataset artefacts.

items.message:
https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22229
*TRIBE (Meta AI):* a multimodal brain encoding model that predicts fMRI responses to naturalistic videos. They extract text (Llama 3.2), audio (Wav2Vec-Bert), and video (V-JEPA 2) embeddings from movie stimuli, fuse them through a transformer encoder with subject-specific output layers, and train on 80+ hours of fMRI from participants watching Friends/movies. The model took 1st place out of 263 teams in the Algonauts 2025 competition, explaining ~54% of explainable brain variance. Key finding: multimodal integration especially benefits high-level associative cortices (prefrontal, parieto-occipital), while primary sensory areas remain largely unimodal.

comments.text: cool paper. Looks like they're predicting parcel level (rather than voxel level) results, but even that is a good starting point. Kind of what to send them an email and see if they'd be open to a collab. I've been wondering about transmodal brain-model convergence a bit, and suspect it may be superior to what we're seeing in mostly vision studies. There are some existing transmodal brain-model convergence studies out there (e.g. Alex Huth has one), but I'm not aware of any involving multimodal models, which can more systematically test brain-model convergence across the cortical hierarchy, which is specifically what I have questions about.

However, their model isn't exactly a typical brain-model convergence study. It seems to be deployed as an instrumental timeseries prediction model, which is potentially useful (the 54% prediction rate is impressive, it suggests BOLD is much less noisy than I thought), but not mechanistically informative in its own right. They're not comparing model representations with brain representations in any kind of transparent way. They're taking their model embeddings (internal representations of the model layers) and then passing those through a second network it seems that they train to predict brain parcel responses so it's likely a highly nonlinear mapping.

They have TribeV2 on the website - a "foundation model" trained to predict cortical dynamics from naturalistic data (movies) using multimodal representations (language/video/i think maybe sound as i recall?). i'm interested in this because it could be the basis for more advanced encoding and decoding models.  better internal brain chunks (complex features).

I think we could train models on hyperaligned data and it might be better.

@member I don’t think hyperalignment is the answer. Hyperalignment is for fine grained intersubject alignment. This is course (parcel based) brain-model alignment. All such evaluations are in some sense already in a high dimensional feature space because models don’t afford any topographies to work with. In this case they use a subject specific linear layer, ie an affine transform, at the end of their encoder model to get to that brain-model mapping (to say nothing of the 8 preceding nonlinear encoder layers). That's more permissive than procrustes so any parcel level hyperalignment you do to the brain data will be negated/anticiapted by that layer and anything you do at the sub parcel level will have no meaningful effect (either you change the mean evoked response via hyperalignment which is biologically uninterpretable, or you use mean invariant hyperalignment and parcel means are left invariant by construction)

Let's take a step back though: what is the point of predicting brain activation? One possibility to design better timeseries estimation tools for fMRI. But I don't think a tech company would throw money at that problem. There are at least two LLM specific questions here too. First, there's a deeper question regarding brain model convergence related to the nature of intelligent systems. You see this interests on both sides (neuro and AI) with the entire CCN crowd on the one hand and the Platonic Representation crowd on the other. Second, I think there's specific interest in the AI community to understand how these models compare with human brain function for the sake of model interpretability, model safety and marketing. Are there are other purposes I might be missing?

For my part I think the model interpretability stuff is the most interesting scientifically. If there are universal principles that span both biological and artificial neural networks that has much greater explanatory power than any instrumental fMRI tool ever could have. So rather than hyperaligning brain data, which is already anticipate by these model architectures, I think a better option is to try something like stepping up the granularity of the encoding model’s prediction from mean parcel timeseries to within-parcel multivariate trajectories with an eye on brain/model interpretability. One way involves simply TR-by-TR RSA, comparing their model activations with local fine scale evoked responses in the brain. This is the approach taken by the most informative brain-model alignment studies in my opinion, like those that compare transformations across model layers with transformations across the ventral visual stream.

You say you want to use these models for stimulus feature extraction. That's only viable if the features the models represents are the same as those the brain represents, but so far there's no guarantee of that. They could diverge in important ways from the brain, in which case whatever features the model produces wouldn't serve as good explanatory vectors for BOLD GLM. Doing the representational analysis is a prerequisite to establish that kind of instrumental use.

The novelty in repeating this exercise with the Meta multimodal model is that most good brain-model alignment studies (which this is paper is not, in my opinion, because it's limited to parcel mean predictions) are limited to individual systems, and often simply applied to the visual system. You could try to do a metaanalysis across these but then you'd be contending with a model zoo: different architectures, learning objectives, schedules, etc. across these papers, which confounds any evaluation of variation acorss brain systems or the cortical hierarchy. Using Meta's model allows for a cross system brainwide evaluation without having to contend with that confound. We can't train a model like that ourselves (they use 128 GPUs to do it, we have ~4), but we should have the hardware to evaluate pretrained model activations and do any necessary post-training.

items.title: TRIBE: TRImodal Brain Encoder for whole-brain fMRI response prediction
items.abstract: Historically, neuroscience has progressed by fragmenting into specialized domains, each focusing on isolated modalities, tasks, or brain regions. While fruitful, this approach hinders the development of a unified model of cognition. Here, we introduce TRIBE, the first deep neural network trained to predict brain responses to stimuli across multiple modalities, cortical areas and individuals. By combining the pretrained representations of text, audio and video foundational models and handling their time-evolving nature with a transformer, our model can precisely model the spatial and temporal fMRI responses to videos, achieving the first place in the Algonauts 2025 brain encoding competition with a significant margin over competitors. Ablations show that while unimodal models can reliably predict their corresponding cortical networks (e.g. visual or auditory networks), they are systematically outperformed by our multimodal model in high-level associative cortices. Currently applied to perception and comprehension, our approach paves the way towards building an integrative model of representations in the human brain. Our code is available at this https URL .
items.summary: The authors introduced TRIBE, a transformer-based deep neural network combining pretrained text, audio, and video foundation models to predict whole-brain fMRI responses to naturalistic video stimuli, winning the Algonauts 2025 competition.
items.key_finding: TRIBE outperformed unimodal models and competitors, especially in high-level associative cortices, by integrating multimodal pretrained representations with a transformer to model spatiotemporal fMRI responses.

classification.notes: Only abstract available; type classified as empirical since it reports new modeling results and competition performance rather than purely a methods paper, though it is method-heavy.

comments.text: How's the reprez drift project going?

It’s on the shelf. I’m not likely to take any initiative with it for six months. I would serve in a secondary role though if someone else has bandwidth to lead it in the meantime. Would like to see cosine similarity measures of evoked responses over time, decoder accuracy breakdown over time, conserved representational geometry using mahalanobis distance based metrics, hyperalignment correcting the imbalance and tracing geodesics on the stiefel manifold as a prospective measure of drift alongside cosine similarity measures.

RSA, hyperalignment and the topological framework are what I’d like to bring to the table. That takes it well outside of the traditional canlab toolkit, so it works best with someone leading who isn’t chained to canlabcore style analysis workflows. As a within person analysis it might be best run in volumetric space though so there’s at least that component, but I’d want it to be kept at the within individual level if done volumetrically. I have fairly low tolerance for choices made on the basis of expediency alone. items.title: Separable and integrated pleasantness coding for appetitive and aversive odors across olfactory and ventral prefrontal cortices
items.abstract: Abstract Odor pleasantness is a key driver of approach and avoidance behaviors, raising the question of how pleasantness is represented in olfactory brain areas. To address this question, here we analyzed an existing dataset consisting of perceptual and fMRI responses to 160 odors from three individual participants. We find that piriform cortex, amygdala, orbitofrontal cortex, and ventromedial prefrontal cortex encode the pleasantness of appetitive and aversive odors. However, whereas these pleasantness representations are separable for appetitive and aversive odors in piriform cortex and amygdala, ventral prefrontal cortex (especially area 11) combines information from appetitive and aversive odors and forms a continuous representation of odor salience. These results suggest that distinct pleasantness codes for appetitive and aversive odors in olfactory cortices are integrated into a continuous representation in ventral prefrontal cortices.
items.summary: Analyzed fMRI responses to 160 odors in three participants and found separable pleasantness codes for appetitive and aversive odors in piriform cortex and amygdala, but integrated continuous salience coding in ventral prefrontal cortex.
items.key_finding: Ventral prefrontal cortex, especially area 11, integrates appetitive and aversive odor pleasantness into a continuous salience representation, unlike the separable codes in piriform cortex and amygdala.

items.message: A perspective on tTIS: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41551-026-01665-z
items.title: Temporal interference stimulation for deep brain neuromodulation in humans
items.abstract: Deep brain stimulation needs high focality in deep parts of the brain; hence, it has largely relied on invasive surgical approaches in clinical populations. Transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) has emerged as a method for focal non-invasive electrical deep brain stimulation. First developed and validated through computational modelling and rodent work, tTIS is now being translated to humans for targeting deep brain regions such as the hippocampus or striatum. Here we present current evidence for tTIS-based neuromodulation, describe the underlying mechanisms and discuss future developments of this technology. We highlight key opportunities and challenges for fundamental neuroscience, as well as for the design of interventions in neuropsychiatric disorders. We suggest that a multidisciplinary research effort is now required to further validate the use of tTIS in multiple applications, understand its underlying principles and optimize the technology in the view of wider scientific and clinical deployment. This Perspective explores how transcranial temporal interference stimulation has been applied to neuromodulate deep brain structures in humans, allowing for the non-invasive study of causal relationships between deep brain regions and behaviour.
items.summary: This perspective reviewed evidence, mechanisms, and future directions for transcranial temporal interference stimulation (tTIS) as a non-invasive method to neuromodulate deep brain structures in humans.

classification.notes: Abstract only; broad review covering multiple applications, so topic tags are approximate given no specific clinical focus stated.

items.message:
"The Illusion of Thinking," which says that AI models, despite their very smart appearance, don't really "understand" or "reason," but just put words together based on statistical patterns to make them seem consistent. Apple tested the most advanced reasoning models in controlled environments and logical puzzles, and found that these models suddenly collapsed as complexity increased, rather than declining. Stranger things, when things get too hard, the model doesn't even try harder, it becomes less reasonable, and it starts to guess. In another experiment, even when the AI was given an accurate step-by-step problem-solving algorithm, it still failed to execute it correctly. The conclusion of the article is that the current models do more "pattern recognition" than real thinking, that is, they overthink simple problems and suffer from a complete lack of logic in complex problems.

https://ml-site.cdn-apple.com/papers/the-illusion-of-thinking.pdf

comments.text: Ya. This is a long standing problem with them. Not sure why this needed to be published, but apparently some people really refuse to accept this scenario, seemingly in defiance of all evidence. The tower of Hanoi demonstrations with unconventional setups were good enough for me.
Oh, there it is too. The tower of Hanoi problem. When was this published?

I "think" whether machines "think" or "feel" like humans is a nonsensical question. Once we have clear criteria for thinking and feeling, we would have to admit that either humans don't think or feel at all, or machines can (will) think and feel (someday).

The question, if I understand it right, is whether neural networks with contemporary architectures are capable of compositional reasoning and if so what it would take to train them to be as proficient at it as a typical human. That isn’t a nonsense question.

My suspicion is that yes they are probably capable in a purely theoretical sense but the training landscape is impossibly complex and we can’t get there with contemporary architectures in any practical sense. New architectures and training strategies may do it.
That said I have seen evidence of compositional reasoning in modern architectures, it’s probably just not prominent enough to be practically useful. I posted about that here August of last year.

items.message: Expected but not experienced delay before painful/non-painful stimuli predicted intensity ratings, by Andreas Strube & Christian Büchel: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-71600-y
items.title: Temporal predictions shape somatosensory perception
items.abstract: Abstract Although intensity expectations have been thoroughly studied in relation to pain, there has been a notable lack of investigation into temporal expectations. One important temporal pain effect, the so-called dread effect, suggests that future pain becomes more aversive with increasing delay. Here we investigated temporal expectations including the dread effect by presenting probabilistically cued painful heat and non-painful cold stimuli after different delay periods. Actual stimulus latency had no effect on perceived intensity in both non-painful cold and painful heat conditions. However, our data clearly show that the expectation of longer delays amplified somatosensory perception, indicating that the dread effect is related to expected and not to experienced delay. Electroencephalography data show that temporal expectations modulate alpha/beta activity during cue presentation, but not during stimulation. Actual stimulus timing is represented in alpha-to-beta frequencies during heat and cold stimulation.
items.summary: Using probabilistic cues and EEG, the authors showed that expected (not actual) delay before painful heat or non-painful cold stimuli amplified perceived intensity, with temporal expectations modulating alpha/beta activity during cue presentation.
items.key_finding: Expectation of longer delays, rather than actual stimulus latency, amplified perceived intensity of both painful and non-painful stimuli, and this dread-like effect was linked to alpha/beta modulation during cue but not stimulation periods.

classification.notes: Only abstract available; approach tags limited to what is described.

items.title: A communication subspace relays context-dependent actions from human prefrontal to motor cortex
items.abstract: Adaptive behavior relies on the ability to translate abstract rules and goals into actions suited to the current context. Neural population activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) has been proposed to support such flexible computations through high-dimensional dynamics, whereas activity in the primary motor cortex (M1) is related more directly to movement execution. How contextual representations in PFC are transformed into ensuing action plans within M1 remains unknown. Previous work suggests that low-dimensional coding subspaces might organize interareal communication, but direct evidence for such population-level communication mechanisms in humans is lacking. Here we use intracranial recordings from human PFC and M1 to identify a communication subspace embedded within high-dimensional PFC activity, that selectively relays behaviorally relevant information at the single-trial level. Activity in this subspace predicts context-dependent action more strongly than either region, revealing a fundamental coding principle by which coordinated interareal population dynamics filter and relay predictive information to guide context-dependent actions. Context-dependent behavior selects actions according to task demands. Using direct brain recordings in humans, Binish et al. uncover how coordinated population activity efficiently channels information from prefrontal to motor cortex.

items.message:
I haven't seen this mentioned here, so I will take a stab at it since it's been popping up in the (tech oriented) news. Less than 2 months ago, in late March, Google released "TurboQuant", an algorithm for compression aimed at reducing bit density of vectors (see here (https://research.google/blog/turboquant-redefining-ai-efficiency-with-extreme-compression/)). This has the makings of a big deal, since it can reduce the memory cost of running LLMs -- especially welcome now, with increasing tightness in the supply of memory chips (I recently saw that investment in AI data centers is up something like 200%, while investment in production of the memory chips and GPUs/CPUs needed to run them is up something like 50%).
Based on Google's results, and some preliminary reimplementations people have started to do, this seems to be a kind of "free lunch" situation: you can reduce the memory footprint, _and_ instead of doing so at the cost of more computation, it actually will simultaneously reduce compute time!
The good:
• No overall high level apparent impact on accuracy
• You can use this with existing models without retooling them 
The ~bad~ skeptical:
• The figures Google provides, like "6x memory reduction", seem to be either highly optimistic, if not inflated, or at least not representative of the total memory use in a typical scenario -- but still, cutting memory by any fraction, without paying a price for it, is still a significant win?
The ~ugly~ other:
• The key pieces here are not new or original; or, put more kindly, the originality here is in bringing together existing things...
    ◦ PolarQuant: representing Cartesian vectors in polar coordinates and quantizing them by dropping precision are both well established approaches
    ◦ Quantized JLT (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2103.00564): the issue with the above is loss of accuracy, and JLT (around for something like 40 years) provides a solution -- randomly rotating vectors -- that will avoid bias in how lower precision quantizes onto your axes, at least in probabilistic and aggregate senses (and the new "Q" part here stores the sign of the error for the quantized version compared to the original in 1 bit, which is used to modify vectors in calculations to reduce the expected error via cancellations).

comments.text:
And, since I asked Gemini for help in understanding the most novel bit (the "Q" above), I will pass along a nicely dumbed down explanation it gave me at once point. (Side note: I got the impression that Gemini has been "advised" to only say nice things about this work, LOL.)
> Imagine you are checking out a massive shipment of 10,000 packages. The scale is broken and rounds every package weight to the nearest 10 pounds (massive compression).
> If you just add up all those rounded numbers, your total will be way off because the rounding errors compound unpredictably.
> Now, imagine a supervisor stands next to the scale and hands you a tiny ticket for each package. The ticket doesn't say the exact weight, it just says *"+"* (it was rounded up) or *"-"* (it was rounded down).
> Because the errors are symmetric, you know the average rounding error is about 2.5 pounds. When you sum up the total shipment, you count up the tickets: for every "+" ticket you subtract 2.5 pounds, and for every "-" ticket you add 2.5 pounds. Because you have a massive sample size, your final calculated total weight will be virtually identical to the true weight.

items.title: An Introduction to Johnson-Lindenstrauss Transforms
items.abstract: Johnson--Lindenstrauss Transforms are powerful tools for reducing the dimensionality of data while preserving key characteristics of that data, and they have found use in many fields from machine learning to differential privacy and more. This note explains what they are; it gives an overview of their use and their development since they were introduced in the 1980s; and it provides many references should the reader wish to explore these topics more deeply.
items.summary: This paper reviewed Johnson-Lindenstrauss transforms, a mathematical technique for dimensionality reduction, tracing their development and applications since the 1980s.

items.title: Multi-focal ultrasound neuromodulation to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex disrupts behavioural and neural pain processing
items.abstract: Abstract Transcranial ultrasound stimulation (TUS) is a promising non-invasive neuromodulation technique for pain-related deep brain regions. This study aimed to investigate neural mechanisms underlying TUS effects on pain processing using neuroimaging. Thirty-two healthy participants underwent two double-blind, randomised sessions (active or sham). A tonic cold stimulus was applied during multifocal TUS applied to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), and during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS). While no significant main effect on pain intensity was observed, active TUS showed a significantly greater reduction in pain ratings between 28- and 55-minutes post-stimulation, suggesting a delayed analgesic effect. Active TUS altered sensory encoding, disrupting the relationship between temperature and pain intensity. There was increased functional connectivity between the dACC and the supplementary motor area, pre-motor cortex, mid-ACC and supramarginal gyrus, and altered salience network connectivity. Overall, these findings suggest dACC-TUS has multidimensional effects across behavioural and neural aspects of pain processing, supporting its potential therapeutic value.
items.summary: A randomised sham-controlled study used multifocal transcranial ultrasound stimulation to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex during fMRI and MRS in healthy participants experiencing tonic cold pain, finding delayed analgesic effects and altered pain-related connectivity.
items.key_finding: Active dACC-TUS produced a delayed reduction in pain ratings (28-55 min post-stimulation), disrupted the temperature-pain intensity relationship, and increased dACC connectivity with SMA, pre-motor cortex, mid-ACC and supramarginal gyrus.

items.message: Closed-loop stimulation modulates attention shifting in children https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-026-02294-0
items.title: Closed-loop stimulation modulates attention shifting in children
items.abstract: Spontaneous fluctuations in attention can impede adaptation to changing goals and environments. Endogenous control over attentional shifts, referred to as attentional flexibility, is prone to disruption in children with attention deficit disorders. Here we studied in vivo intracranial recordings in children with epilepsy to identify a reproducible neural signature of attentional control that could predict and prevent impending lapses in real time. Machine learning classifiers were trained on intracranial signals while each child performed an attentional set-shifting task and predicted delays in attention shifting over multiple days and across several pediatric populations. Intracranial electrical stimulation in response to impending delays rescued attention shifts indexed by eye tracking, reaction time and accuracy. Simultaneous electroencephalography identified corresponding scalp signatures that enabled noninvasive modulation of attention shifting in healthy participants. These findings provide insight into the neural basis of attentional shifts with implications for targeted neuromodulation and exogenous attentional control. Intracranial recordings in children revealed neural signals predicting attentional lapses. Closed-loop stimulation rescued performance and scalp EEG enabled noninvasive modulation, identifying a reproducible marker of attentional control.
items.summary: Researchers used intracranial recordings and machine learning in children with epilepsy to detect neural signatures predicting attentional lapses, then applied closed-loop electrical stimulation to rescue attention shifting, later replicated noninvasively with scalp EEG.
items.key_finding: Closed-loop intracranial stimulation triggered by machine-learning-predicted attentional lapses restored attention shifts (measured via eye tracking, reaction time, accuracy), and corresponding EEG signatures enabled noninvasive modulation in healthy participants.

NeuroAgent: LLM Agents for Multimodal Neuroimaging Analysis and Research
https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06584 (https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.06584)
items.title: NeuroAgent: LLM Agents for Multimodal Neuroimaging Analysis and Research
items.abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging analysis often involves complex, modality-specific preprocessing workflows that require careful configuration, quality control, and coordination across heterogeneous toolchains. Beyond preprocessing, downstream statistical analysis and disease classification commonly require task-specific code, evaluation protocols, and data-format conventions, creating additional barriers between raw acquisitions and reproducible scientific analysis. We present NeuroAgent, an LLM-driven agentic framework that automates key preprocessing and analysis steps for heterogeneous neuroimaging data, including sMRI, fMRI, dMRI, and PET, and supports interactive downstream analysis through natural-language queries. NeuroAgent employs a hierarchical multi-agent architecture with a feedback-driven Generate-Execute-Validate engine: agents autonomously generate executable preprocessing code, detect and recover from runtime errors, and validate output integrity. We evaluate the system on 1,470 subjects pooled across all ADNI phases (CN=1,000, AD=470), where all subjects have sMRI and tabular data, with subsets also having Tau-PET (n=469), fMRI (n=278), and DTI ($n=620$). Pipeline ablation studies across multiple LLM backends show that capable models reach up to 100% intent-parsing accuracy, with the strongest backend (Qwen3.5-27B) reaching 84.8% end-to-end preprocessing step correctness. Automated recovery limits manual intervention to edge cases where human review is required via the Human-In-The-Loop interface. For Alzheimer's Disease classification using automatically preprocessed multimodal data, our agent ensemble achieves an AUC of 0.9518 with four modalities, outperforming all single-modality baselines. These results show that NeuroAgent can reduce the manual effort required for neuroimaging preprocessing and enable end-to-end automated analysis pipelines for neuroimaging research.
items.summary: NeuroAgent, an LLM-driven multi-agent framework, automated preprocessing and analysis of multimodal neuroimaging data (sMRI, fMRI, dMRI, PET) and achieved 0.9518 AUC for Alzheimer's classification using ADNI data.
items.key_finding: An LLM agent ensemble automatically preprocessing four modalities achieved AUC=0.9518 for Alzheimer's classification, outperforming single-modality baselines, with the best backend reaching 84.8% end-to-end preprocessing accuracy.

*Three parsimonious spatiotemporal patterns in cerebellum reveal individual traits in function and behavior* (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-72931-6 ) : Spatiotemporal patterns derived from complex PCA correlate with empirical functional connectivity topographies, and sex, cognitive, emotional, alertness and personality traits.

A related study (*A parsimonious description of global functional brain organization in three spatiotemporal patterns*: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41593-022-01118-1) showed previously that complex PCA-derived spatiotemporal patterns underlie "functional connectivity gradients, the task-positive/task-negative anti-correlation pattern, the global signal, time-lag propagation patterns, the quasiperiodic pattern and the functional connectome network structure".

comments.text: @member Looks like they use do spatiotemporal PCA in the complex domain in that first paper. This methodology could appeal to your aesthetic interests and might be applicable to HRF grant aims in the lab.

In related news, a preprint today shows that spatiotemporal electrophys decoding from the ventral visual stream is more effective for category decoding than spatial information alone. The HRF creates an opportunity to pursue something similar with fMRI in the sense that we could do spatiotemporal decoding instead of spatial decoding alone, and see how it compares. This has been more inspired by Churchland's population dynamics perspective (2012 Nature) than the idea of feedforward/feedback connections along the ventral visual stream, but this paper is a much more direct parallel of the kind of analysis I'm proposing. You could cite this as precedent from the electrophys the same way Tor cites Georgoupolus 1986 as inspiration for purely spatial MVPA.

Paper itself isn't a major breakthrough though. It's something that's been anticipated for a long time (e.g. the notion that early unimodal cortex operates as high resolution buffer; Lee 1996 Vision Research), but as a demonstration of the virtues of spatiotemporal decoding in a domain typically subjected to spatial analysis it may nevertheless be a useful precedent:

https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12825

Ah, I see - this is interesting. So they made a complex analytic function by adding the hilbert transform. I just took a cursory glance but it seems that can allow them to capture temporal lags in functional connectivity using the imaginary part. But I am curious to know how would they make sense of the lags - whether its neural or vasculature based. I do think it can be useful for HRFs too

Isn’t the hilbert transform just a convenient way to get phase and amplitude info in coarse sampled data where a Fourier basis would entail a bunch of tedious arithmetic due to the awkward sampling intervals?

Right - it has been a while since I have dived into this, but I think one should be able to do the same using Fourier bases. Apart from QM I think, any complex analysis can be replaced by real analysis in higher dimensions. And my complaint about not being able to separate neural vs. vasculature stuff in functional connectivity holds true in general.

But aside from this, I think Hilbert transforms maybe massively susceptible to noise. Like if you are relying on phase information of a low snr broadband signal like BOLD, preprocessing itself will start influencing things. So I am not sure how reproducible things would be. At the very least I'd be wary of using it on small datasets. I wonder if the tedious fourier basis approach would be more robust.

I don't know the theoretical details myself either. My only contact with the Hilbert transform in a research capacity was in AFNI's retinotopy mapping software where it's more robust than the fourier basis approach for estimating the phase of periodic evoked responses (the canonical retinotopic mapping stimulus is a periodic sweep of the visual field so phase maps to position in that visual field). I've never had any formal training in signal processing...
Yeah, no wonder this is more useful for EEG like analysis. I used to see old fMRI papers where people cared about phases.

items.title: Three parsimonious spatiotemporal patterns in cerebellum reveal individual traits in function and behavior
items.abstract: The cerebellum plays a critical role in large-scale brain functional connectivity structure and synchronizing global waves propagation. Despite extensive studies on cortical spatiotemporal architecture, particularly in zero-lag and time-lag synchrony, leaving the parsimonious cerebellar representational structure largely overlooked. Using complex principal component analysis (CPCA) on resting-state fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project, we delineate three dominant low-dimensional spatiotemporal patterns within the cerebellum, manifesting as unimodal-to-transmodal progression, functional antagonism, and hemispheric asymmetry. These patterns correlate with various empirical functional connectivity topographies, including functional connectome network structure, quasiperiodic pattern, functional connectivity gradients and brain network dynamics hierarchy. Importantly, functional connectivity reconstructed from these patterns preserves the intrinsic structural modularity, proving the robustness of the sparse cerebellar dynamics. Moreover, personalized CPCA-derived features enable accurate sex classification and prediction of cognitive, emotional, alertness and personality traits. Our findings position the cerebellum as an active, trait-sensitive integrator of brain-wide spatiotemporal organization, suggesting propagation-based motifs constitute a foundational mode of individual brain intrinsic function. In this study, the authors identify three dominant cerebellar spatiotemporal patterns that preserve structural modularity, integrate whole-brain functional organization, and predict sex as well as cognitive, emotional, alertness, and personality traits.
items.summary: Using complex principal component analysis on resting-state fMRI from the Human Connectome Project, researchers identified three dominant cerebellar spatiotemporal patterns that predicted sex, cognitive, emotional, and personality traits.
items.key_finding: Three cerebellar spatiotemporal patterns (unimodal-to-transmodal progression, functional antagonism, hemispheric asymmetry) preserved structural modularity and enabled accurate sex classification and trait prediction.

items.title: Reconsidering Brain Age: Why Age-Prediction Models Fail as Measures of Brain Aging
items.abstract: Brain age models - machine-learning predictions of chronological age from brain imaging - are widely interpreted as markers of accelerated brain aging. Here we show that this interpretation cannot be supported. Because these models are trained to predict chronological age, they prioritize features that change similarly across people and actively downweight features that capture differences in individual trajectories, precisely the property an aging-rate biomarker must have. In effect, brain age models are optimized to ignore the very signal they are used to study, thereby risking converting stable between-person differences into apparent accelerated aging. Using theoretical analysis, simulations, and longitudinal MRI, we confirm both predicted failure modes: brain age models indicated "accelerated aging" in participants with low birth weight despite no longitudinal evidence, while a single hippocampal volume measurement was more sensitive than the brain age gap to tau-related neurodegeneration. Across much of the brain age literature, it is therefore not possible to determine whether reported effects reflect brain aging or stable anatomical differences, and the brain age gap should not be interpreted as a marker of brain aging or brain health. We propose alternative strategies that reorient prediction targets from shared age-related patterns to individual differences in change. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. ### Funding Statement This study was funded by South-Eastern Norway Regional Health Authority (to EG [HSO-2021079]), the Department of Psychology, University of Oslo (to KW, AF), the Norwegian Research Council (to KW, AM, DP [ES694407]) and the project has received funding from the European Research Council's Starting Grant scheme (to \textit{AF}[283634, 725025] and KW [313440]). ### Author Declarations I confirm all relevant ethical guidelines have been followed, and any necessary IRB and/or ethics committee approvals have been obtained. Yes The details of the IRB/oversight body that provided approval or exemption for the research described are given below: The ethics committee of the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, the Dallas Lifespan Brain Study, the Harvard Aging Brain Study, the Pre-symptomatic Evaluation of Experimental or Novel Treatments for AD study, the Center for Lifespan Changes in Brain and Cognition cohort and UK Biobank gave ethical approval for this work. I confirm that all necessary patient/participant consent has been obtained and the appropriate institutional forms have been archived, and that any patient/participant/sample identifiers included were not known to anyone (e.g., hospital staff, patients or participants themselves) outside the research group so cannot be used to identify individuals. Yes I understand that all clinical trials and any other prospective interventional studies must be registered with an ICMJE-approved registry, such as <http://ClinicalTrials.gov|ClinicalTrials.gov>. I confirm that any such study reported in the manuscript has been registered and the trial registration ID is provided (note: if posting a prospective study registered retrospectively, please provide a statement in the trial ID field explaining why the study was not registered in advance). Yes I have followed all appropriate research reporting guidelines, such as any relevant EQUATOR Network research reporting checklist(s) and other pertinent material, if applicable. Yes The raw data were gathered from many different datasets. Different agreements are required for each dataset. Most datasets are openly available with prespecified data usage agreements. For some datasets, such as UKB, fees may apply. See the Supplementary Material for a detailed description of how to access the data.

items.key_finding: Brain age models falsely indicated accelerated aging in low-birth-weight participants despite no longitudinal evidence, while hippocampal volume alone outperformed brain age gap in detecting tau-related neurodegeneration.

items.title: A shared code for perceiving and imagining objects in human ventral temporal cortex
items.abstract: Mental imagery allows us to remember previous experiences and imagine new ones. Animal studies have yielded rich insight into mechanisms for visual perception, but the neural mechanisms for visual imagery remain poorly understood. We determined that approximately 80% of visually responsive single neurons in the human ventral temporal cortex (VTC) use a distributed axis code to represent objects. We used that code to reconstruct objects and generate maximally effective synthetic stimuli. We then recorded responses from the same neural population while subjects imagined specific objects; about 40% of axis-tuned VTC neurons recapitulated the visual code. Our findings reveal that visual imagery is supported by reactivation of the same neurons involved in perception, providing single-neuron evidence for the existence of a generative model in human VTC.
items.summary: Researchers recorded single neurons in human ventral temporal cortex during object perception and imagery, finding a shared distributed axis code underlying both processes.
items.key_finding: About 40% of axis-tuned VTC neurons that represented perceived objects also reactivated during imagination of those same objects, supporting a generative model of imagery.

items.title: Plasticity and language in the anaesthetized human hippocampus
items.abstract: Consciousness is a fundamental component of cognition1, but the degree to which higher-order pattern recognition relies on it remains disputed2,3. Here we demonstrate the persistence of oddball discrimination, semantic processing and online prediction in individuals under general-anaesthesia-induced loss of consciousness4,5. Using high-density Neuropixels microelectrodes6 to record both single-unit and local-field-potential neural activity in the human hippocampus while playing a series of tones to anaesthetized patients, we found that hippocampal neurons and local oscillations retained some detection of oddball tones. This effect size grew over the course of the experiment (around 10 min), demonstrating representational plasticity. A biologically plausible recurrent neural network model showed that learning and oddball representation are an emergent property of flexible tone discrimination. Moreover, when we played language stimuli, single units and local field potentials carried information about the semantic and grammatical features of natural speech, even predicting semantic information about upcoming words. Together these results indicate that in the hippocampus, which is anatomically and functionally distant from primary sensory cortices7, complex processing of sensory stimuli occurs even in the unconscious state. In the hippocampus, complex processing of sensory stimuli occurs even in the unconscious state.
items.summary: Recording single-unit and local-field-potential activity from human hippocampus during general anaesthesia revealed persistent oddball detection and semantic/grammatical processing of speech despite loss of consciousness.
items.key_finding: Hippocampal neurons and oscillations showed growing oddball discrimination and predictive semantic processing of language during anaesthesia-induced unconsciousness, supported by a recurrent neural network model of emergent learning.

items.message:
Cool new paper (Lee et al., PNAS 2026):
New noninvasive stimulation method (twtACS) that creates a directional propagating electric field across the cortex by phase-shifting currents across electrodes. They validate the cortical electric fields with intracranial recordings, show in an NHP that it shifts population spike timing in a direction-specific way (standard tACS does not, despite stronger entrainment), and in humans find a clean dissociation: forward twtACS improves memory encoding, backward improves visual attention, matching known endogenous TW dynamics for each task.
Main point: traveling wave direction causally controls cognition. Nice tool for probing this.
https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2527296123 (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2527296123)​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​
items.title: Traveling-wave transcranial alternating current stimulation (twtACS) causally links neural timing to cognitive function
items.abstract: Cortical traveling waves (TWs) are brain oscillation patterns that support the transfer of neural information across distinct brain regions, with their direction shaping cognitive function. However, direct evidence for their causal influence on brain dynamics and behavior remains lacking. Here, we establish such a causal link by externally applying TW-like electric field patterns. To achieve this, we develop a noninvasive brain stimulation protocol, traveling-wave transcranial alternating current stimulation (twtACS). twtACS can generate a precise directional electric field that propagates across the cortical surface, which we validate using human intracranial recordings. In monkey recordings, we show that neural spiking was directionally modulated, shifting systematically across space in line with the direction of twtACS. In humans, twtACS led to direction-dependent improvements in cognitive performance. Together, these findings demonstrate that externally imposed TWs can causally shape neural activity and cognition, highlighting the potential of twtACS as a neuromodulation technique for cognitive enhancement.
items.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
items.summary: Researchers developed traveling-wave transcranial alternating current stimulation (twtACS) and showed it causally directs cortical traveling waves, modulating monkey neural spiking and improving human cognitive performance in a direction-dependent manner.
items.key_finding: twtACS produced directional electric fields that shifted monkey neural spiking spatially and caused direction-dependent improvements in human cognitive performance.

"Our analysis of T1 MRI data from 46,381 UK Biobank participants reveals that simpler machine learning models [ridge regression], and notably those with excessive regularization [alpha > 1000], demonstrate superior sensitivity to disease-relevant changes compared to their more complex counterparts [CNN & visual transformers], despite being less accurate in chronological age prediction."
https://journals.plos.org/plosbiology/article?id=10.1371/journal.pbio.3003451
items.title: Brain-age models with lower age prediction accuracy have higher sensitivity for disease detection
items.abstract: This study critically reevaluates the utility of brain-age models within the context of detecting neurological and psychiatric disorders, challenging the conventional emphasis on maximizing chronological age prediction accuracy. Our analysis of T1 MRI data from 46,381 UK Biobank participants reveals that simpler machine learning models, and notably those with excessive regularization, demonstrate superior sensitivity to disease-relevant changes compared to their more complex counterparts, despite being less accurate in chronological age prediction. This counterintuitive discovery suggests that models traditionally deemed inferior might, in fact, offer a more meaningful biomarker for brain health by capturing variations pertinent to disease states. These findings challenge the assumption that accuracy-optimized brain-age models serve as useful normative models of brain aging. Optimizing for age accuracy appears misaligned with normative aims: it drives models to rely on low-variance aging features and to deemphasize higher-variance signals that are more informative about brain health and disease. Consequently, we propose a recalibration of focus towards models that, while less accurate in conventional terms, yield brain-age gaps with larger patient-control effect sizes, offering greater utility in early disease detection and understanding the multifaceted nature of brain aging.
items.summary: Analysis of T1 MRI brain-age models in 46,381 UK Biobank participants found that simpler, more regularized models with lower chronological age prediction accuracy showed greater sensitivity to disease-related brain changes.
items.key_finding: Models less accurate at predicting chronological age produced brain-age gaps with larger patient-control effect sizes, indicating better disease detection utility than accuracy-optimized models.

items.message:
ANN-like back propagation of errors is famously biologically implausible. One reason is because in ANNs you pass forward the entire signal, compute the loss, and then pass it all back. This kind of temporal segregation doesn't occur in the brain, at least not with the kind of granularity needed to fine tune microcircuits (DA does it with a time delay at a coarser scale, but signal routing decisions are fixed by anatomy, not task contingencies, so it's not well suited for microcircuit level modifiable and differential selectivity).

In this new paper (came out yesterday, but submitted 3+ years ago!? :face_with_spiral_eyes:) an equivalent method for credit assignment is identified that separates teaching signals along dendritic compartments as opposed to temporally (recall, dendrites are leaky and the impact of stimuli at distal dendrites is not the same as for proximal dendrites, enabling computational flexibility as a function of where synaptic events occur). This offers a biologically plausible analogue to back prop for the cortex via cortico-cortical feedback connections.

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-026-10190-7
items.title: Vectorized instructive signals in cortical dendrites
items.abstract: Vectorization of teaching signals is a key element of almost all modern machine learning algorithms, including backpropagation, target propagation and reinforcement learning. Vectorization allows a scalable and computationally efficient solution to the credit assignment problem by tailoring instructive signals to individual neurons. Recent theoretical models have suggested that neural circuits could implement single-phase vectorized learning at the cellular level by processing feedforward and feedback information streams in separate dendritic compartments1–5. This presents a compelling, but untested, hypothesis for how cortical circuits could solve credit assignment in the brain. Here we used a neurofeedback brain–computer interface task with an experimenter-defined reward function to test for vectorized instructive signals in dendrites. We trained mice to modulate the activity of two spatially intermingled populations (four or five neurons each) of layer 5 pyramidal neurons in the retrosplenial cortex to rotate a visual grating towards a target orientation while we recorded GCaMP activity from somas and corresponding distal apical dendrites. We observed that the relative magnitudes of somatic and dendritic signals could be predicted using the activity of the surrounding network and contained information about task-related variables that could serve as instructive signals, including reward and error. The signs of these putative teaching signals depended on the causal role of individual neurons in the task and predicted changes in overall activity over the course of learning. Furthermore, targeted optogenetic perturbation of these signals disrupted learning. These results demonstrate a vectorized instructive signal in the brain, implemented via semi-independent computation in cortical dendrites, unveiling a potential mechanism for solving credit assignment in the brain. Mice learning a neurofeedback brain–computer interface task show neuron-specific teaching signals in cortical dendrites, consistent with a vectorized solution for credit assignment in the brain.

Good read. This seems quite connected to your preprint, which I assume is why you sent it. He does note that subtle differences can occur, and as such, there may be slight differences in how the system performs the computation (maybe different inference or different assumption embedded idk):

"Diverse models and brains are universal in that they learn to represent major variance-explaining latent factors of the sensory data...While their representations may share major variance-explaining latent factors, the subtle differences between them can reveal the unique computational mechanisms that each system uses to perform tasks effectively with limited resources."

I hope they continue on this at CCN 2026. I am hoping to go. @member

I was trying to judge the preprints timeliness and identify other people on social media who are in a similar space atm to follow, which is how I came across this. So ya, it’s related. I got to thinking about this stuff while talking over cover letter and framing strategies with Tor and Martin the other day. I’ve submitted my paper though so there’s no direct relevance for it except that it inspired this search that led to this doc.

Re: CCN, it was basically an RSA conference in its first few years and it’s still largely represented so one way or another I expect you’ll have stuff like this there.

I'm surprised this is considered out of the loop for this space, but I guess it is relative to people's backgrounds and interests.

That would actually be super interesting to me. I have some funding to try and go and it seems like a good fit (financially and interest wise). What has been your experience at CCN? And have others in the lab gone?

A bunch of people went when it was in Boston in 2024. 2023 it was just Heejung and I. 2025 it was just me. It alternates between north america and europe every year, which is partially what explains the discrepancy. I ran into Phil Kragel there last year among CANLab associates. Emily Finn speaks highly of it too and is often in attendance. A lot of Jim's people go. Erica Busch has been at every one I've attended, Feilong and Jiahui have been at many. It's potentially my favorite conference and competes for that designation with COSYNE.

COSYNE is more animal work + ANNs + theory, CCN is more human work/psychology + ANNs + theory. COSYNE is older, more competitive, and better established. I learn more at COSYNE I think but I present and network better at CCN.

For my part I intend to attend these conferences as often as I can justify. This year I haven't been productive enough though to submit stuff to either unfortunately, and we'll see what kind of conference funding I have available next year.

Whether you'll benefit or not, that's hard for me to tell. I don't really know what your curriculum was, nor how much you've been able to pick up by osmosis from these lab experiences. For my part coming out of undergrad these conferences were totally off my radar and far afield from what I had studied. I do think they're among the hottest conferences in ?neuroscience? today though, and that if you're engaging with ideas like neural representations, neural coding principles, artificial neural net learning dynamics, brain-model alignment, and so on, then these could be very constructive places for continuing education, networking and presenting work.
