items.title: Identification and characterization of genetic risk shared across 24 chronic pain conditions in the UK Biobank.
items.abstract: Chronic pain is attributable to both local and systemic pathology. To investigate the latter, we focused on genetic risk shared among 24 chronic pain conditions in the UK Biobank. We conducted genome-wide association studies (GWAS) on all conditions and estimated genetic correlations among them, using these to model a factor structure in Genomic SEM. This revealed a general factor explaining most of the shared genetic variance in all conditions and an additional musculoskeletal pain-selective factor. Network analyses revealed a large cluster of highly genetically inter-connected conditions, with arthropathic, back, and neck pain showing the highest centrality. Functional annotation (FUMA) showed organogenesis, metabolism, transcription, and DNA repair as associated pathways, with enrichment for associated genes exclusively in brain tissues. Cross-reference with previous GWAS showed genetic overlap with cognition, mood, and brain structure. In sum, our results identify common genetic risks and suggest neurobiological and psychosocial mechanisms of vulnerability to chronic pain. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest. ### Funding Statement This study was funded by R01 DA046064: "Brain and Genetic Predictors of Individual Differences in Pain and Placebo Analgesia" ### Author Declarations I confirm all relevant ethical guidelines have been followed, and any necessary IRB and/or ethics committee approvals have been obtained. Yes The details of the IRB/oversight body that provided approval or exemption for the research described are given below: The North West Multi-centre Research Ethics Committee gave ethical approval for the collection of human data (UK Biobank) obtained by authors via an application to the UK Biobank and used in this study. I confirm that all necessary patient/participant consent has been obtained and the appropriate institutional forms have been archived, and that any patient/participant/sample identifiers included were not known to anyone (e.g., hospital staff, patients or participants themselves) outside the research group so cannot be used to identify individuals. Yes I understand that all clinical trials and any other prospective interventional studies must be registered with an ICMJE-approved registry, such as <http://ClinicalTrials.gov|ClinicalTrials.gov>. I confirm that any such study reported in the manuscript has been registered and the trial registration ID is provided (note: if posting a prospective study registered retrospectively, please provide a statement in the trial ID field explaining why the study was not registered in advance). Yes I have followed all appropriate research reporting guidelines and uploaded the relevant EQUATOR Network research reporting checklist(s) and other pertinent material as supplementary files, if applicable. Yes All data produced in the present study are available upon reasonable request to the authors.

items.title: A Bayesian Model for Chronic Pain
items.abstract: The perceiving mind constructs our coherent and embodied experience of the world from noisy, ambiguous and multi-modal sensory information. In this paper, we adopt the perspective that the experience of pain may similarly be the result of a probabilistic, inferential process. Prior beliefs about pain, learned from past experiences, are combined with incoming sensory information in a Bayesian manner to give rise to pain perception. Chronic pain emerges when prior beliefs and likelihoods are biased towards inferring pain from a wide range of sensory data that would otherwise be perceived as harmless. We present a computational model of interoceptive inference and pain experience. It is based on a Bayesian graphical network which comprises a hidden layer, representing the inferred pain state; and an observable layer, representing current sensory information. Within the hidden layer, pain states are inferred from a combination of priors p(pain), transition probabilities between hidden states p(pain_{t+1}|pain_{t}) and likelihoods of certain observations p(sensation|pain). Using variational inference and free-energy minimization, the model is able to learn from observations over time. By systematically manipulating parameter settings, we demonstrate that the model is capable of reproducing key features of both healthy- and chronic pain experience. Drawing on mathematical concepts, we finally simulate treatment resistant chronic pain and discuss mathematically informed treatment options.
items.summary: The authors developed a Bayesian graphical model of interoceptive inference to explain how chronic pain arises from biased priors and likelihoods, and simulated treatment-resistant pain states.
items.key_finding: Systematic manipulation of model parameters reproduced key features of both healthy and chronic pain experience, including treatment-resistant pain.

classification.notes: Only abstract available; classified as empirical since it presents and tests a computational model via simulation.

Press release from NCCIH on Lada and @member's paper.

comments.text: We should discuss this paper in JC someone else should present though because I'm too critical of it, but I'd like to discuss it.
Curious to hear what you think about it :)

There's a paper from 2018 that looks at interindividual variability in resting state functional connectivity and the results map to pain pretty well (attached, figure 5 panel "individual" is key and shows differences between individuals in functional connectivity). I've been able to reproduce these findings myself and shown that they can be resolved with connectivity hyperalignment, and here is the key. Resolving differences in functional connectivity also resolves idiosyncracies in pain evoked response patterns between individuals, meaning that the differences between individuals are not pain specific: pain evoked response differences are explained by differences in spontaneous activity at rest.

You guys show the greatest differences in multivariate patterns in vlpfc, dlpfc, vmpfc, precuneus, etc. Higher order areas. These are the same areas that show high variability in resting state functional connectivity in gratton 2018, and several of them map to areas where resting state hyperalignment is able to resolve differences between individuals. I've been presenting preliminary findings on this at a couple of conferences in the past year, but here's a poster from one attached. I'm still waiting to extend the analysis to subcortex and cblm before publishing it, but it's in the works.

This would suggest that there's a higher order invariance relationship that's conserved across individuals, and it's at the level of high dimensional functional geometry, not at the level of fine scale topography. If that's true then it suggests the more parsimonious geometric perspective is a better model of fine scale representations in the brain and that the naive topography may be the wrong way to look at this entirely.

Your network analysis on top of the RDM is fascinating to me though, and teases some of my more fanciful speculations about brain function lately. One issue that arises in high dimensional geometric approaches to brain function is how to integrate local high dimensional flexibility with local anatomical constraints. presumably differences in cytoarchitecture constrain the location of brain function at a coarse level but at a finer scale level developmental considerations like those I outlined above leave a lot of room for flexibility. These two characteristics of brain physiology don't have any clear reconciliation in the literature. In hyperalignment there's this tendency to simply brush it under the rug by applying alignment to individual searchlights and averaging the results over searchlight overlaps. Others try to restrict their analysis to individual brain parcels, although this of course is limited by the accuracy of the parcel boundaries. Your network analysis of RDMs is very suggestive that there is in fact some kind of interlocking pattern to functional tography of neighboring structures, perhaps similar to a crystalline latice structure.

Hey @member thanks for your thoughtful comments. I don’t have enough time to respond right now, but will do when I have some time. All of your comments are valid IMO, but we also thought many of those and tried to address them in multiple ways (and through revisions). But yes, there may be some fundamental limitations that we should address in the future.

and if you could share citation for the following comment, that would be really helpful!
> SVM is especially problematic because its bias is quite opaque (Bayesian methods are best because the bias is formally specified, but even pcr has a well characterized bias, however esoteric it may be, if interested I can give you the citation).

And I totally agree with you that our ultimate goal is to get generative models, but as you know, it's extremely difficult to get it with fMRI (though we should keep trying). I think what we did is the best we can do with biased, but predictive (and thus potentially useful) models.

> There's no behavioral correlate to any of this variability, so how do we know any of it matters? This is a major limitation of this study because there are multiple sources of fine scale topographic variability between conspecifics that we know are of no practical relevance.
Yep, I totally agree! Honestly, I never thought this work could be published in NN because of this limitation (no behavioral correlates). :slightly_smiling_face: But this time what I learned is that the academic fields really long for conceptual advancements even with some limitations (like this one). At the same time, from some preliminary analyses (that were included in our response letters), we've got a lead on that. We hope that we can provide some evidence on behavioral correlates of the ind variability of regional patterns.

> meaning that the differences between individuals are not pain specific: pain evoked response differences are explained by differences in spontaneous activity at rest.
Yes, this is totally possible. We haven't argued that the individual variability that we found is not specific to pain. Yes, I believe it could reflect more fundamental brain architecture, which is why we included the principal gradient interpretation in the paper.

> several of them map to areas where resting state hyperalignment is able to resolve differences between individuals.
Cool!

> This would suggest that there's a higher order invariance relationship that's conserved across individuals, and it's at the level of high dimensional functional geometry, not at the level of fine scale topography. If that's true then it suggests the more parsimonious geometric perspective is a better model of fine scale representations in the brain and that the naive topography may be the wrong way to look at this entirely.
Very interesting! I also believe that the information geometry will have the answer to all these. Yes, I agree that I may be scratching only the surface (i.e., BOLD signal pattern topography) now, and we need to go deeper into the neural information and their computational principles, which I really want to examine in the future. I'm developing a new line of research targeting these.. so let's talk. Some of my students are studying information geometry, generative models, and esp. adopting ideas from monkey neurophys work from the dynamical systems view. E.g., At CCN this year, we are presenting a result of applying the conditional VAE models on pain fmri data, and at SfN, we are presenting work on the subspace alignment analysis of the expectation-induced pain modulation (in collaboration with Dr. Seng Bum Michael Yoo from Jazayeri lab). Oh, and I'm also collaborating with Dr. SueYoun Chung at NYU on manifold geometry for multimodal processing in pain. All these new directions are really in line with your comments, I think. Let's talk. :slightly_smiling_face:

What's the advantage of using SVM as the basis here? You claim that only some of your models (in some subjects) are significantly predictive but whether they are or are not doesn't affect your results. What would be lost if you used univariate GLM models instead of SVM? Each voxel could “predict” pain outcome, and granted they wouldn't be as good of predictions as a multivariate model but why does that matter when your non-significantly predictive SVM models show the same results as your predictive ones? If multivariate predictions are important why not choose a method with a more transparent bias than SVM? Say PCR or PLS which basically fits a model to a smoother version of the data (loosely speaking)? Or alternatively simply treat the univariate weights as a multivariate map? (Isnt this like performing a multivariate regression with a diagonal covariance matrix? So biased but also transparent). I get that the potential diagnostic value of these models is attractive to journal editors and readers but you're either studying individual differences in predictive models or individual differences in physiology, and my impression (maybe I'm mistaken) is that you're interested in the physiology here, not simply in a technical report on SVM applied to pain.
NN’s interest in this is indeed interesting and thought provoking.

Cool. Seems there's some convergence in our thinking here. I'll also be at sfn. Looking forward to seeing you there. I'm not presenting results related to this there but I do have relevant data to show that we can look at.
Tagged you in the post regarding pcr bias

Thanks, @member. We used the SVR for no reason, actually. Lada just used it, and I did nothing because I was okay with it. There were two reasons that I thought it's okay to use SVR. 1) From my previous experience, if we are using the full components, solutions from PCR vs. SVR were almost identical. Because I didn't plan to use the reduced number of components for the analysis (though the number of trials should serve as a limit for the number of components), I predicted the solutions from the SVR vs. PCR should be very similar. 2) Given that the numbers of trials were different across studies, if we're using PCR, we ended up using different numbers of components across studies.

> What would be lost if you used univariate GLM models instead of SVM?
Hm.. my reasoning was that with multivariate predictive modeling, we should be able to get more sensitivity and specificity in identifying the important contributors to pain prediction. Using univariate models instead of SVM would be interesting, but I am not sure if it is going to be better at identifying individual differences in physiology. I've seen many results where multivariate methods provide much more sensible maps even from the perspective of physiology.

> why does that matter when your non-significantly predictive SVM models show the same results as your predictive ones?
Hm.. what we tested was that even with the non-significant models, the results on the individual variability of predictive weights were similar to without those. And I think there were only small proportion of participants who had non-sig models. Not sure we're on the same page on this.
It's possible I misunderstood the significance of the non-significant models… no pun intended.

I'm very skeptical about multivariate models producing better models than univariate models “in terms of physiology”. If true this deserves some thought. All multivariate methods in widespread use in neuroimaging are biased. If biased methods were to produce “better models” it would be very counter intuitive.

I’d love to hear more about what you mean by “bias”. In addition, I’m curious to hear why you think biased methods produce worse models if we come to physiology.

“Bias” usually helps with generalizability (in bias-variance tradeoff), and thus it could provide better models in general. It prevents overfitting and facilitates learning if there are few observations, right?

Even for physiology or neuronal-level models, bias (if they are carefully and correctly implemented) can help, right? E.g., all neural network models that are working well (e.g., CNN, RNN, etc.) are biased, I think.

But maybe here we use the term, “bias” differently, so I’d love to hear why you think biased methods will produce worse models for physiology.

And it feels like the issue here seems more related to the debate on “encoding” vs. “decoding” models… but I could be wrong.

Sure.

When you fit a model that fitting procedure yields estimates of the model parameters. Assuming the model is correct and you're estimating the right parameters you would expect your estimates to be close to the "true" values. Of course this isn't always the case. Your estimates will be wrong by some amount. But you at least hope that they're as likely to overshoot as to undershoot the true value, and that the error is small. OLS doesn't guarantee a small error, but it does guarantee that it will on average over repeated implementations give you estimates that are centered on the true value. Each time you sample a particular n from a population and estimates the model you may overshoot in your estimates, or undershoot, but you will do so equally and in the long run these overshoots and undershoots cancel out because they're centered on the true parameter value. This is what's meant when we say the “expected outcome is the true value” or things like that. 

Bias violates these principles. It means you're not equally likely to overshoot as to undershoot because your model estimation procedure does not center itself over the true parameter values, but rather has a tendency to drift towards a particular value that is not the true value of the process you're trying to estimate. We accept this outcome because in exchange we can often increase model stability, which has various practical benefits, but in the process we lose the ability to claim insight into the true underlying parameter values.

Ridge regression is an easy context where you can understand this. You may have 100 parameters x1 .. x100 in your model, and a sample size of 50. You can fit that using ridge regression, and you will get a bunch of small and mostly similar estimates across all parameters. Say though that the true generating process is x1 = 1, and xn = 0 for n = 2-100. You can take samples of 50 from your population an infinite number of times and estimate a model, and your mean model will never be centered on the true parameter values because ridge regression will tend to underestimate x1 and overestimate all remaining x.

The predictions you get from the model will be useful, but you would never use the model to infer whether a particular xn is "significant", because of this bias. Take a moment here to imagine if you had used ridge regression instead of SVMs in your paper, and you may begin to better understand my objection at the beginning of this thread.

The nice thing about ridge is that you can understand bias here in terms of bayesian priors, because it's just bayesian regression with an Normal(mu = 0, sigma) prior, but bias also exists for pcr, svr, and any other non-OLS method.

You're thinking of the benefits of generalizability in terms of a measurement produced by a model. And that's fine. It is helpful there. But as for the model's parameters, they're systematically wrong.

You can use such models to learn things about physiology, but IMO (and it's only an opinion, someone more clever than me might be able to figure out a loophole) they cannot be used to directly inform physiology through their pattern weights. There's a difference for instance between a map of searchlight SVM performance tiling the brain and a map of an SVM model's weights projected to the brain. Only the former informs physiology. The latter simply shows you the model mechanics so you can critically evaluate whether it's going to be trustworthy and when it's going to potentially fail.

This perspective of course has not been standard in Tor's group, nor among those who learn mvpa here, but the machine learning literature is unambiguous on these points, and I've been trying to raise awareness and correct this oversight internally for a couple of years now.
The key point is that what informs physiology in a brain based ML model is the predictive value, not the model parameters.
I see what you're saying. Thanks for this. I need to think more about, then, how to improve our approaches. Esp. how to use mvpa to inform physiology/mechanisms...

Thanks for the discussion. Bogdan, I think you've defined bias as I would in your Ridge example above. But  biases, to the extent they exist (eg. Ridge and Lasso), are (1) intentional, (2) an effect of the cost function used [related to ridge/lasso shrinkage], and (3) don't render the coefficients uninterpretable in terms of underlying physiology [or, more generally, which predictors are important].

Consider Lasso: shrinkage is imposed to make some coefficents drop to 0. Others that remain are often interpreted as important -- both for prediction and in terms of underlying psychology/biology/whatever. Imagine you run a regression with predictors of age, smoking , and physical activity on cardiovascular health.  Age drops to zero and the others are significant. You can't say for sure that there's *no* effect of age, but you can interpret the others as having non-zero effects if they are statistically significant, with or without LASSO.  Introducing a bias towards zero is not particularly problematic in terms of interpreting positive findings.   @member @member

In part it seems like you're arguing that multiple regression is "biased", which I don't think is right. ie. if you use a bunch of brain features in OLS regression to predict an outcome, the slopes are still BLUE -- best linear unbiased estimators. it's only biased when you introduce shrinkage, but this is generally considered to aid interpretation rather than reduce it. That was point of developing LASSO in the first place after all (in the original Tibshirani paper).

You might be arguing that principal component reduction or other procedures (in SVR) introduces some more complex kind of bias, though (1) I'm not sure that's true in terms of expected results [i do remember some of our discussions], and (2) I'm not sure it's problematic in terms of interpreting positive findings. I maintain that the interepretation of univariate GLM is a relationship without controlling for other brain variables, and multivariate (with OLS/multiple regression or shrinkage and/or component reduction)  shows relationships controlling for other brain variables in some fashion (though imperfectly and different depending on the algorithm/etc).

As in the Haufe 2014 paper and earlier papers on structure coefficients, I think that both are useful when interpreting multiple regressions and neither is a perfect way of making the correct causal inferences when there are many intercorrelated variables (which is just very very hard in principle, perhaps impossible).

@member this may have been an incomplete post (it seems truncated at the end), so forgive me if I misrepresent what you're saying or didn't get the full picture, but I have misgivings about your stance. When you say that biased models "don't render the coefficients uninterpretable in terms of underlying physiology" I take issue. Are you interested in understanding the relative contribution of that physiology to psychology, behavior, or some other natural process, or are you interested in understanding how physiology drives your prediction machine? Only the latter seems valid.

Supposing you've got predictive lasso weights that say all of pain prediction is driven by ACC. If this were an unbiased model, then you might be reasonably justified in attempting an intervention which would inhibit ACC activity to reduce pain. This is not justified on the basis of a lasso model though. If you correctly interpret your lasso weights you would never expect an intervention in acc to completely abolition pain based on that model. You however seem to believe that it would justify a belief that intervening in ACC function might have some effect. Maybe. It sounds plausible, but can you prove it? I'm not sure this has a proof in the literature, therefore I doubt that it is justified, and for my part I'm hesitant to make the assumption absent such proof. It may be though, but any proof would necessarily need to appeal to the nature of the bias in lasso. It is not a claim that applies to machine learning algorithms in general. [Edit: And at any rate, the model would be expected to overestimate the efficacy of any such intervention due to its bias.]

You claim that a significant model weight would serve as evidence of a true contribution of a brain area to a natural process, but as a counter example, to demonstrate that this claim does not apply generally to biased models, consider a ridge model which shows pain is widely distributed throughout the brain (this is a plausible model fit given a sufficiently small sample). According to your logic, the nonzero weights of an ML model (ridge in this case) should indicate areas that do in fact reflect the biology of pain. Does this mean that intervening anywhere in the brain will affect pain? No. Ridge weights will be full of false positives due to the role of the bias term in 'flattening' weights across model parameters.

And to be clear, here I'm referring to the claim you make when you write "You can't say for sure that there's *no* effect of age, but you can interpret the others as having non-zero effects if they are statistically significant, with or without LASSO." I believe that IF this nonzero ML weights reflect biology for LASSO, then that is simply a peculiar feature of LASSO. It does not apply to biased models generally. Meanwhile, an OLS model showing significant weights might reasonably support belief that intervention in those brain areas should affect the natural process because the gauss-markov theorem proves that the expected parameter estimate of OLS is the true value of the generating process.

LASSO and Ridge however are not the models we or wani use. We use PCR, SVR, PLS, etc. Lasso and Ridge are particularly convenient models because we can formally specify the nature of their biases (laplace distribution on the weights and normal distribution on the weights, resp). If positive weights in lasso regression were to justify belief that a brain area is implicated in a natural process then it would be precisely this ability to formally specify lasso biases which would allow us to understand the relationship between their biased weights and physiology. Meanwhile, our understanding of the irrelevance of ridge weights also comes from an intuitive understanding of its biases (and any formal proof of their irrelevance would likely appeal to this bias formally). In most cases we are using models where "we" (your average neuroimaging practitioner using these methods) do not understand the biases (had you read that chemometrics paper I shared with Wani on PCR bias before publishing the NEJM results? Does Wani or the first author on the NN paper understand the biases of SVR? I believe the answer to both questions is "no" and that this is typical for neuroimaging). In some cases I'm not sure the biases are even understood by ML specialists (and I suspect this most for SVM, because of the various methods I've attempted to understand this one seems the most opaque; I don't even know where to begin to grasp it). In such cases, including PCR, PLS and SVR, I believe our ability to understand the relationship between a biased weight and physiology breaks down completely. All we can claim is that a particular physiological feature drives the model predictions. We cannot claim anything about that physiological feature in particular and our construct of interest. 

There is a difference between understanding what kind of physiology drives your biased model's behavior and understanding the underlying biological system. Meanwhile, this discrepancy does not extend to unbiased models, where model weights both inform the behavior of your model and can rightfully be seen as a fair attempt at understanding the underlying biological system.
@member @member

Tor, I think you're confusing a number of issues here. On the one hand there is univariate vs. multivariate modeling, on the other hand there is biased vs unbiased modeling and lastly there's interpretable modeling vs uninterpretable modeling.

I do not object to multivariate modeling. I think the source of the confusion here may be in the language. I talk about how I approve of OLS and advocate its use, but OLS is often used as a shorthand for univariate GLM. I am not using it to refer to univariate GLM. Univariate GLM is fit with OLS, but multiple regression parameters are also estimated using OLS, and it is the latter I have in mind, although both are valid in my book and neither are biased.

Interpretability is useful in some instances, especially instrumental model development, but when we are interested in understanding generative processes, like the biological correlates of a behavior, percept or cognitive state, interpretability is secondary to estimating the generative process correctly. This is the case in Wani's NN paper, and it is the case in most neuroimaging papers. The process itself may be simple, in which case interpreting the unbiased model would be easy, or it may be intrinsically complex, and estimating that complexity would take precedence over forcing simplicity upon the model to ease interpretation. At least if what you care about is an accurate characterization of biology rather than tool building. 

Tbshirani's example is not valid in this scenario where we want to estiamte generative processes. Tbshirani was looking to develop a variable section method when he wanted a parsimonious model so that the model's behavior could be understood. This is particularly valuable when you're more interested in the predictions than in how they are obtained and are willing to subordinate accuracy in the estimation procedure for a better understanding of the outcome. This is the scenario confronted in some niche neuroimaging applications, but it is not typical. Examples that come to mind including predicting non-brain related outcomes from brain variables (e.g. socioeconomic status in a caste based society). Why you would do this given the expense of poor SNR of fMRI is unclear, but maybe you want to draw some kind of secondary inferences from some public dataset like UK biobank or something and that's all you had to work with. Notably the NEJM paper does develop an instrumental model, which is valuable first and foremost for its predictive abilities, and you might be willing to subordinate model accuracy for predictive utility. However, the use of LASSO there does not actually facilitate interpretability because it's applied to the latent principle component space, while interpretation is happening in the voxel space which is still complex and not parsimonious. Moreover,  the NEJM paper overextends itself by attempting to draw inference on the underlying generative process, and this is invalid because the weights are biased. It many ways it's the source of this problem I'm trying to address now, and has caused all sorts of problems downstream in papers that were inspired by it.

You speculate @member that causal inference in a multivariate context may be impossible. I would deny this unequivocally. OLS allows for causal inference in a multiple regression in the same manner that causal inference is done based on univariate measures in a traditional GLM. To the extent to which traditional GLM allows for causal inference then so does multiple regression, and although there are philosophical objections to drawing causal inference from GLM (correlation is not causation, etc) I do not believe those are issues that are relevant to our disagreements here (I think you wani and I are all willing to concede that correlation is not causation while nevertheless winking and nodding suggestively towards causation and multiple regression at least meets the burden of proof for that). I sense that you would cite the difficulty of accurately estimating the covariance structure of data that is highly collinear. This is not in fact a problem for sufficiently large datasets. There are some limitations to OLS in the presence of collinear variables, but I don't think it's a bias issue, I think it's a variance problem, and I believe it's still solved in the limit of large n, but perhaps n >> p (n is sample size, p is model dimensions). If you're looking for a more practical solution than collecting datasets much much larger than the number of voxels you're working with, you can simply use PCR and as long as n > p it is both unbiased and more robust (lower variance) in the presence of collinear variables. This is not simply a theoretical point, It's a roadmap for how one might go about doing unbiased multivariate modeling on searchlights, regions or otherwise constrained subspaces where the constraints can be justified theoretically a priori.

The way I see things fmri aspires to unbiased multivariate models of brain processes. We need more data than we can obtain to do this. Consequently we've historically used univariate models to answer the simpler question regarding whether or not a brain area is implicated in a process without focusing on models which also incorporating information on how areas interact. Having exhausted all the low hanging fruit with this approach we're now investigating what we can learn from a decoding model about information content in specific brain regions and across the brain, but we still can't properly estimate a fully multivariate model of brain function that is accurate. A lot of confusion about multivariate methods stems from the tradition of using univariate methods to localize function based on parameter estimates but multivariate biased models represent a different paradigm entirely where it is the predictive accuracy and not the parameter estimates which characterize the underlying function. Searchlight SVM is an exemplary version of this approach, although claiming you can dissociate signals for noxious from vicarious pain may be a more familiar example which seems just as good and to work for the same reason: it's conclusions stem from the interpretation of predictive accuracy rather than model weights.

items.title: Adaptive Empathy: A Model for Learning Empathic Responses in Response to Feedback
items.abstract: Empathy is usually deployed in social interactions. Nevertheless, common measures and examinations of empathy study this construct in isolation from the person in distress. In this article we seek to extend the field of examination to include both empathizer and target to determine whether and how empathic responses are affected by feedback and learned through interaction. Building on computational approaches in feedback-based adaptations (e.g., no feedback, model-free and model-based learning), we propose a framework for understanding how empathic responses are learned on the basis of feedback. In this framework, adaptive empathy, defined as the ability to adapt one’s empathic responses, is a central aspect of empathic skills and can provide a new dimension to the evaluation and investigation of empathy. By extending existing neural models of empathy, we suggest that adaptive empathy may be mediated by interactions between the neural circuits associated with valuation, shared distress, observation-execution, and mentalizing. Finally, we propose that adaptive empathy should be considered a prominent facet of empathic capabilities with the potential to explain empathic behavior in health and psychopathology.
items.summary: The authors proposed a theoretical framework called 'adaptive empathy,' arguing that empathic responses are learned through feedback via model-free and model-based learning mechanisms during social interactions.

classification.notes: Theoretical/review paper proposing a computational framework; no new empirical data reported in abstract.

items.abstract: Can studying individual differences in brain structure and function reveal individual differences in behavior? items.title: Augmented pain inhibition and higher integration of pain modulatory brain networks in women with self-injury behavior
items.abstract: Abstract Individuals who engage in nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI) have demonstrated insensitivity to pain compared with individuals without NSSI. Yet, the neural mechanisms behind this difference are unknown. The objective of the present study was to determine which aspects of the pain regulatory system that account for this decreased sensitivity to pain. In a case–control design, 81 women, aged 18–35 (mean [SD] age, 23.4 [3.9]), were included (41 with NSSI and 40 healthy controls). A quantitative sensory testing protocol, including heat pain thresholds, heat pain tolerance, pressure pain thresholds, conditioned pain modulation (assessing central down-regulation of pain), and temporal summation (assessing facilitation of pain signals) was used. Pain-evoked brain responses were assessed by means of fMRI scanning during thermal pain. NSSI participants showed a more effective central down-regulation of pain, compared to controls, assessed with conditioned pain modulation. The neural responses to painful stimulation revealed a stronger relation between nociceptive and pain modulatory brain regions in NSSI compared to controls. In line with previous studies, pressure and heat pain thresholds were higher in participants with NSSI, however, there were no correlations between pain outcomes and NSSI clinical characteristics. The augmented pain inhibition and higher involvement of pain modulatory brain networks in NSSI may represent a pain insensitive endophenotype associated with a greater risk for developing self-injurious behavior.
items.summary: A case-control fMRI and QST study found that women with nonsuicidal self-injury showed enhanced central pain inhibition and stronger connectivity between nociceptive and pain modulatory brain networks compared to controls.
items.key_finding: Women with NSSI showed more effective conditioned pain modulation and higher pain thresholds, alongside stronger integration between nociceptive and pain modulatory brain regions, suggesting a pain-insensitive endophenotype.

classification.notes: Abstract only; specific brain regions and connectivity methods not detailed.

items.title: C﻿ommunicating doctors’ consensus persistently increases COVID-19 vaccinations
items.abstract: Abstract The reluctance of people to get vaccinated represents a fundamental challenge to containing the spread of deadly infectious diseases 1,2 , including COVID-19. Identifying misperceptions that can fuel vaccine hesitancy and creating effective communication strategies to overcome them are a global public health priority 3–5 . Medical doctors are a trusted source of advice about vaccinations 6 , but media reports may create an inaccurate impression that vaccine controversy is prevalent among doctors, even when a broad consensus exists 7,8 . Here we show that public misperceptions about the views of doctors on the COVID-19 vaccines are widespread, and correcting them increases vaccine uptake. We implement a survey among 9,650 doctors in the Czech Republic and find that 90% of doctors trust the vaccines. Next, we show that 90% of respondents in a nationally representative sample ( n = 2,101) underestimate doctors’ trust; the most common belief is that only 50% of doctors trust the vaccines. Finally, we integrate randomized provision of information about the true views held by doctors into a longitudinal data collection that regularly monitors vaccination status over 9 months. The treatment recalibrates beliefs and leads to a persistent increase in vaccine uptake. The approach demonstrated in this paper shows how the engagement of professional medical associations, with their unparalleled capacity to elicit individual views of doctors on a large scale, can help to create a cheap, scalable intervention that has lasting positive impacts on health behaviour.
items.summary: A large-scale survey and randomized field intervention in the Czech Republic showed that correcting public misperceptions about doctors' trust in COVID-19 vaccines persistently increased vaccine uptake.
items.key_finding: Providing accurate information about doctors' 90% trust in COVID-19 vaccines corrected widespread underestimation and led to a lasting increase in vaccination rates over 9 months.

classification.notes: This paper is outside CANlab's typical neuroscience focus; tagged based on closest matching categories (social/clinical/behavioral).

<!channel> Etienne Vachon-Presseau is giving a talk that's just started on chronic pain subtyping using brain imaging and the UK Biobank data. Relevant to several of you I think.
*Title: A multivariate model for classifying and predicting different pain conditions in the UK Biobank*

*Presented by: Dr. Etienne Vachon-Presseau, Assistant Professor, Pain and Neuroscience, Faculty of Dental Medicine and Oral Health Sciences, (https://www.mcgill.ca/dentistry/) McGill University, Canada*
 
*Abstract: Predictive modeling is becoming increasingly popular in the quest of personalized medicine. Previous studies have suggested that chronic pain conditions can be determined from the interactions between physiological, psychological, social, cognitive, affective, and behavioral factors. Despite its popularity, the elements composing the biopsychosocial model for chronic pain remain hard to define due to the difficulties of simultaneously measuring multidimensional factors in large groups of pain patients. More importantly, the evidence that the framework is useful to forecast chronic pain conditions remains to be demonstrated. Recent accessibility to large cohorts of chronic pain patients provides unprecedented opportunities to tackle these problems. Here, we used machine learning on a curated series of 99 features selected in the UK Biobank and derived a model that predicted the number of co-existing pain sites, classified chronic pain conditions, and forecasted individual differences in the spreading of chronic pain nine years later. Our model generalized to secondary outcomes such as general health, disability, opioid use, and a wide range of non-cancer illnesses. A risk score derived from the model was associated with three pre-selected biological factors available in the biobank, namely, an inflammatory blood marker, a polygenic risk score computed for the number of pain sites, and a neuroimaging-based marker for sustained pain. Overall, our results provide empirical evidence that a multivariate framework trained on pain-agnostic features can predict different chronic pain conditions in out-of-sample patients.*
 *Zoom Link:* https://us02web.zoom.us/j/85027785392?pwd=WjgrQUFTWmNZQ0tFL1A4NTdSOGJFdz09
*Meeting ID: 850 2778 5392*
*Password: Models*

comments.text: Thanks - sorry i missed this. I saw a student of his present on this work, but the abstract seems somewhat different. @member was it one model that predicted these various things?  And what was the "neuroimaging marker for sustained pain"?  I wonder if you saw this @member @member @member @member and have a sense of how it relates to our earlier/ongoing efforts?

So I missed a key section due to technical difficulties on my end, but he explored both a psychosocial model and a brain based model. His neuroimaging marker was very black box. He pushed the idea of prediction > explanation and didn't delve into the mechanism of the brain marker. It was a combination of fMRI, T1 and DTI data, and it looked like the fMRI data was collapsed across time by conversion into a covariance matrix or graph matrix (seemed like he had both as distinct inputs into the model)

One interesting point is that he used similar approaches to explain other conditions in the biobank data that might have intenesting neural correlates like parkinsons or MS, so he presented a very nice comparison of the relative strength of these different signals in the brain imaging data, and chronic pain was bottom of the barrel
However he was able to predict pain outcomes years later, and he did so better the more pain sites a subject associated with their chronic pain

@member @member From what I was able to make, I thought it was a really great talk, and definitely gave some important insights on phenotypic analyses in the UKB.  Sadly, I missed the first bit but caught the last half. Hoping to catch up on the recording. A big takeaway I got was that brain phenotypes were actually not predictive of chronic pain conditions, except to the extent that head movement influenced the brain phenotypes, and chronic pain patients appeared to move much more in the scanner. They had a hypothesis that head movement could be one of the better predictors of chronic pain, but I don't think they tested it. Tor, you definitely brought this idea up in a paingen meeting! I am actually not sure yet how they isolated head movement, but I guess you can do that from the raw data?
Overall really cool stuff, and excited to hopefully discuss more in an upcoming paingen meeting.

items.title: The brain structure and genetic mechanisms underlying the nonlinear association between sleep duration, cognition and mental health
items.abstract: Sleep duration, psychiatric disorders and dementias are closely interconnected in older adults. However, the underlying genetic mechanisms and brain structural changes are unknown. Using data from the UK Biobank for participants primarily of European ancestry aged 38–73 years, including 94% white people, we identified a nonlinear association between sleep, with approximately 7 h as the optimal sleep duration, and genetic and cognitive factors, brain structure, and mental health as key measures. The brain regions most significantly underlying this interconnection included the precentral cortex, the lateral orbitofrontal cortex and the hippocampus. Longitudinal analysis revealed that both insufficient and excessive sleep duration were significantly associated with a decline in cognition on follow up. Furthermore, mediation analysis and structural equation modeling identified a unified model incorporating polygenic risk score (PRS), sleep, brain structure, cognition and mental health. This indicates that possible genetic mechanisms and brain structural changes may underlie the nonlinear relationship between sleep duration and cognition and mental health. Change in sleep patterns is an important feature of the aging process. This study shows that sleep duration is nonlinearly associated with mental health and cognition measures in the 38- to 73-year-old population, with underlying brain and genetic mechanisms.
items.summary: Using UK Biobank data, researchers found a nonlinear relationship between sleep duration and cognition/mental health, mediated by brain structure and polygenic risk factors.
items.key_finding: Approximately 7 hours of sleep was optimal, with insufficient or excessive sleep associated with cognitive decline, mediated by precentral cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, and hippocampal structure and genetic risk.

items.title: Negativity bias, personality and political ideology
items.abstract: Research suggests that right-wing ideology is associated with negativity bias: a tendency to pay more attention and give more weight to negative versus positive stimuli. This work typically relies on either self-reported traits related to negativity bias in large, often-representative, samples or physiological and behavioural indicators of negativity bias in small convenience samples. We extend this literature and examine the relationship of negativity bias to political ideology using five distinct behavioural measures of negativity bias in four national samples of US residents with a total analytical sample size of about 4,000 respondents. We also examine the association of these behavioural measures to four of the most common self-report measures of personality in the literature on ideology. Across a wide range of tests, we find no consistent evidence for a relationship of negativity bias to either ideology or self-reported personality. Across five studies, Johnston and Madson find no support for the hypothesis that people with right-wing political views are more sensitive to negative and threatening stimuli than people with left-wing political views.

items.message:
A new paper showing that belief polarization can happen even when prior beliefs are not biased and the decision-making process is optimal, and there is no social influence, simply when people are asked to make binary decisions between two options and are balancing between accuracy and speed. And that these effects disappear (or are weaker) when the goal is to estimate how strongly the data supports one of the options rather than decide between them. It suggests that one of the main reasons for polarization is that people are forced to take sides, rather than acknowledge the complexity and the relative strength of evidence.
I found it very interesting and also potentially relevant for connecting election beliefs (they cite it) with PPRI (effects of data sampling on perception). I believe you will find it interesting too @member

items.title: A multistudy analysis reveals that evoked pain intensity representation is distributed across brain systems
items.abstract: Information is coded in the brain at multiple anatomical scales: locally, distributed across regions and networks, and globally. For pain, the scale of representation has not been formally tested, and quantitative comparisons of pain representations across regions and networks are lacking. In this multistudy analysis of 376 participants across 11 studies, we compared multivariate predictive models to investigate the spatial scale and location of evoked heat pain intensity representation. We compared models based on (a) a single most pain-predictive region or resting-state network; (b) pain-associated cortical–subcortical systems developed from prior literature (“multisystem models”); and (c) a model spanning the full brain. We estimated model accuracy using leave-one-study-out cross-validation (CV; 7 studies) and subsequently validated in 4 independent holdout studies. All spatial scales conveyed information about pain intensity, but distributed, multisystem models predicted pain 20% more accurately than any individual region or network and were more generalizable to multimodal pain (thermal, visceral, and mechanical) and specific to pain. Full brain models showed no predictive advantage over multisystem models. These findings show that multiple cortical and subcortical systems are needed to decode pain intensity, especially heat pain, and that representation of pain experience may not be circumscribed by any elementary region or canonical network. Finally, the learner generalization methods we employ provide a blueprint for evaluating the spatial scale of information in other domains.
items.summary: Analyzed 376 participants across 11 studies to compare multivariate models predicting evoked pain intensity from single regions, networks, multisystem models, or whole brain, using cross-validation and holdout validation.
items.key_finding: Distributed multisystem brain models predicted pain intensity 20% more accurately than any single region or network, with no additional benefit from full-brain models.

items.title: Comprehensive decoding mental processes from Web repositories of functional brain images
items.abstract: Abstract Associating brain systems with mental processes requires statistical analysis of brain activity across many cognitive processes. These analyses typically face a difficult compromise between scope—from domain-specific to system-level analysis—and accuracy. Using all the functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging (fMRI) statistical maps of the largest data repository available, we trained machine-learning models that decode the cognitive concepts probed in unseen studies. For this, we leveraged two comprehensive resources: NeuroVault—an open repository of fMRI statistical maps with unconstrained annotations—and Cognitive Atlas—an ontology of cognition. We labeled NeuroVault images with Cognitive Atlas concepts occurring in their associated metadata. We trained neural networks to predict these cognitive labels on tens of thousands of brain images. Overcoming the heterogeneity, imbalance and noise in the training data, we successfully decoded more than 50 classes of mental processes on a large test set. This success demonstrates that image-based meta-analyses can be undertaken at scale and with minimal manual data curation. It enables broad reverse inferences, that is, concluding on mental processes given the observed brain activity.
items.summary: Trained neural network models on tens of thousands of NeuroVault fMRI statistical maps labeled with Cognitive Atlas concepts to decode over 50 mental process categories from unseen brain images.
items.key_finding: Machine-learning models successfully decoded more than 50 classes of mental processes across a large heterogeneous test set of fMRI images from NeuroVault.

items.title: Meta-matching: a simple framework to translate phenotypic predictive models from big to small data
items.abstract: There is significant interest in using brain imaging data to predict non-brain-imaging phenotypes in individual participants. However, most prediction studies are underpowered, relying on less than a few hundred participants, leading to low reliability and inflated prediction performance. Yet, small sample sizes are unavoidable when studying clinical populations or addressing focused neuroscience questions. Here, we propose a simple framework – “meta-matching” – to translate predictive models from large-scale datasets to new unseen non-brain-imaging phenotypes in boutique studies. The key observation is that many large-scale datasets collect a wide range inter-correlated phenotypic measures. Therefore, a unique phenotype from a boutique study likely correlates with (but is not the same as) some phenotypes in some large-scale datasets. Meta-matching exploits these correlations to boost prediction in the boutique study. We applied meta-matching to the problem of predicting non-brain-imaging phenotypes using resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC). Using the UK Biobank (N = 36,848), we demonstrated that meta-matching can boost the prediction of new phenotypes in small independent datasets by 100% to 400% in many scenarios. When considering relative prediction performance, meta-matching significantly improved phenotypic prediction even in samples with 10 participants. When considering absolute prediction performance, meta-matching significantly improved phenotypic prediction when there were least 50 participants. With a growing number of large-scale population-level datasets collecting an increasing number of phenotypic measures, our results represent a lower bound on the potential of meta-matching to elevate small-scale boutique studies. ### Competing Interest Statement The authors have declared no competing interest.

items.title: SARS-CoV-2 is associated with changes in brain structure in UK Biobank
items.abstract: Abstract There is strong evidence of brain-related abnormalities in COVID-19 1–13 . However, it remains unknown whether the impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection can be detected in milder cases, and whether this can reveal possible mechanisms contributing to brain pathology. Here we investigated brain changes in 785 participants of UK Biobank (aged 51–81 years) who were imaged twice using magnetic resonance imaging, including 401 cases who tested positive for infection with SARS-CoV-2 between their two scans—with 141 days on average separating their diagnosis and the second scan—as well as 384 controls. The availability of pre-infection imaging data reduces the likelihood of pre-existing risk factors being misinterpreted as disease effects. We identified significant longitudinal effects when comparing the two groups, including (1) a greater reduction in grey matter thickness and tissue contrast in the orbitofrontal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus; (2) greater changes in markers of tissue damage in regions that are functionally connected to the primary olfactory cortex; and (3) a greater reduction in global brain size in the SARS-CoV-2 cases. The participants who were infected with SARS-CoV-2 also showed on average a greater cognitive decline between the two time points. Importantly, these imaging and cognitive longitudinal effects were still observed after excluding the 15 patients who had been hospitalised. These mainly limbic brain imaging results may be the in vivo hallmarks of a degenerative spread of the disease through olfactory pathways, of neuroinflammatory events, or of the loss of sensory input due to anosmia. Whether this deleterious effect can be partially reversed, or whether these effects will persist in the long term, remains to be investigated with additional follow-up.
items.summary: Longitudinal UK Biobank MRI study of 785 participants found greater brain structural changes and cognitive decline in those infected with SARS-CoV-2 compared to controls.
items.key_finding: SARS-CoV-2 infection was associated with greater loss of grey matter thickness in orbitofrontal cortex and parahippocampal gyrus, tissue damage in olfactory-connected regions, greater global brain size reduction, and greater cognitive decline, even after excluding hospitalized cases.

items.message:
This paper is useful reference supporting the argument that MVPA may accurately reconstruct underlying neuronal population dynamics. The authors specifically show that manifolds can be reconstructed from multiunit activity without spike sorting. Multiunit activity usually intermingles responses from different neurons within any particular recording channel, and normally spike sorting is used to transform this into a multi-neuron response pattern. Then population codes are computed from that to construct response manifolds. This paper shows that you can build these population code manifolds directly from the multiunit activity without first identifying individual neurons, and that the results match the ones reconstructed from identified neuron's activity almost perfectly. The result is far from sufficient to show that MVPA can recover population code manifolds, but it is necessary.

The implications for MVPA applications to fMRI come from the fact that we obviously only measure mixtures of neural signals, similar to unsorted multiunit activity in a sense: individual neural activity is summed within voxels and noninvertably transformed by vascular signals. Notably, the authors show that sparser sampling of neurons is better than denser sampling of neurons because it results in a larger amount of uncorrelated activity. This allows for better reconstruction of latent dimensions of population code manifolds. In other words, low spatial resolution (to a point) may actually be an advantage, not a disadvantage for fMRI. In fact, this paper actually models how one might quantify what's lost (or not) at different resolutions or using different measurement modalities in the last section of the results.

The paper demonstrates these points by reanalyzing data from several studies of motor cortex function. This context is relevant to the theoretical justifications Tor often uses for MVPA, since he cites Georgeopolis, et al. (1986) Science to support his interpretation of behavioral embeddings in population codes. Georgeopolis is a study that relates neural population codes to peripheal movement parameters (direction, velocity, etc). To understand the current paper it is important to be familiar with some critical developments in theories regarding motor cortex population codes that have occurred since then. A key paper is Churchland, et al. (2012) Nature, which shows that motor cortex population codes in macaque do not directly represent movement parameters (and this is one of the studies this paper analyzes, the same person is senior author on that paper as here). This has lead to a competing perspective on population codes which is summarized well by the digest to this article (itself a replication of Chuchland, in humans): https://elifesciences.org/articles/07436 (scroll down to just below the abstract). Reading this digest should be sufficient to head off any confusion you might otherwise have with the current article if you're coming from the older Georgeopolis perspective.

The authors show that the results will hold anytime "the neural activity manifold is relatively low dimensional and smooth across time, and the tuning properties of neurons on the same electrode are not strongly anticorrelated". When individual neurons are anticorrelated within a channel their signals cancel out due to interference, hence that last requirement. This kind of anticorrelation is uncommon in their data.

This could potentially be a good journal club article, but for my part I won't have time to prepare it this week. Between the focus on animal studies (a weakness of sorts in the lab), and the way the article may serve as a semi review of recent relevant literature (the 3 studies they replicate), in a context that's directly relevant to the methods we use, it would be a good study for anybody who might be interested in leading a journal club. Such a journal club would need at least 90 minutes, but ideally 2 hours.

And btw, motor control is probably more relevant to what we do than computational models of perceptual systems (e.g. vision), since it's subject to internal control and direction like emotion, motivation, beliefs, etc. It's frontal cortex function at any rate.

comments.text:
Hi Bogdan, thanks for this detailed explanation! It’s very interesting in terms of the fundamentals of neural coding.  It makes me realize how complex the relationships between primary motor activity and muscle activity, and other parameters of movements that humans care about, are!  

I’m still not sure what the “ cyclic, dynamic patterns” they find in the motor cortex actually represent. That is, how does population activity in a state space relate to movement of a muscle , position of a joint , movement direction, etc.? Maybe more answers are in the papers…

@member I also struggle with understanding these models of cortical dynamics. One paper that was somewhat helpful was a review from one of these motor dynamics groups, Gallego et al. (2017) Neuron (attached). Here's a relevant excerpt,

"Single neuron ... experiments sought explicit representations that relate single-neuon activity to ... target position, endpoint and and joint kinematics, endpoint forces, and muscle activity (Evarts, 1968; Georgopoulos et al., 1982; Hum- phrey et al., 1970; Morrow et al., 2007; Thach, 1978). ... they were restricted to models of non-interacting neurons whose individual activity was associ- ated with specific movement covariates.

However, some single neurons ... did not represent movement parameters ... If neurons in primary motor cortex (M1) were to represent movement parameters, those representations ought to be most evident in corticomotoneuronal (CM) cells, which make direct connections onto spinal motoneurons. Yet, many ... do not represent any specific movement covariate.

The ultimate role of M1 is to generate movement, not to represent it (Churchland et al., 2012; Cisek, 2006; Scott, 2004); thus, it is not surprising that manyM1 neurons do not relate to any single movement covariate. The search for representations at the sin- gle-neuron level might actually divert us from understanding the neural control of movement. Early neural network simulations indicated that individual neurons need not explicitly encode movement covariates when the goal of M1 population activity is to generate realistic muscle activation patterns (Fetz, 1992).

The role of neurons that do not explicitly represent any movement covariate can be explained by recent work based on optimal feedback control theory, which postulates that the goal of motor cortex is to produce a desired movement and force, taking into account the state of the muscles."

There is an argument that's specifically relevant to the motor cortical cyclical dynamics that's not described in this paper that may also be helpful though. That argument is that the grasping behavior studied in these motor papers evolved from a different and still dominant form of cyclic motor activity (locomotion is an obvious example of this, whether in a single celled organism or in bipeds), which is then repurposed into non-cyclic motor behavior for many routine tasks (or alternatively cyclic behavior that lasts for less than a full period of the cycle). The idea is that something like rhythmic stimulation of the relevant muscles at different frequencies leads to the asymmetries in excitation needed to affect a desired motor action. Churchland, et al. (2012) Nature talk about this in their intro, and demonstrate that EMG activity in deltoid muscles can be explained as a linear combination of an oscillatory basis recorded from M1 during reaching behavior.

Kriegeskorte has also shown how sinusoidal activity of two or more neurons with different frequency or phase can lead to cyclic manifolds in his 2021 Nat Rev Neurosci paper, but it's straightforward if you think about relationships between sinusoidal functions in cartesian coordinates (e.g. the plot of x = sin(z), y = cos(z) = sin(pi/2 - z), x is one neurons firing rate, y is the other's, the trigonometric identity shows how they're simply out of phase, and then you plot them in cartesian coordinates to get a circle).

I don't think these kinds of dynamical systems are limited to motor cortex though. I've been looking at motor cortex because I suspect it's a good model of cortical activity that is self directed as opposed to stimulus driven, and that some of those principles may apply to a number of higher order processes common to tasks that implicate frontal cortices more generally (or at least poke holes in models entirely inspired by sensory processing).

Here's an example of 'cyclic, dynamic patterns' in neurons in and around frontal eye field in monkeys, during a task where the monkeys needed to make a cue-contingent choice between a left or right saccade, with the cue indicating whether the choice should depend on the motion or color of a stimulus. The authors show that the PFC neurons they record from transiently integrate both color and motion information, but weigh their choice only in terms of the relevant parameter. Using a recurrent neural network model they show that they can produce the exact same behavior in the network without any notable architectural constraints, allowing them to then study the artificial network directly to understand how it's affected by cue information. If I understand it correctly, they find the cue information shifts the space within which the neural dynamics propagate and that in one domain of the state space only motion information weighs their response whereas in the other domain only color information weighs the response. The authors don't call the resultant dynamics 'cyclical, dynamic patterns', but compare figure 2a and 2f with Churchland, et al. (2012) Nature. It jumps out at you.

Granted, FEF is still a motor area due to its control of eye muscles, but unlike in Churchland and related studies, the activity recorded here doesn't seem to be directly responsible for muscle control. Motor control is matched between task contingencies, so whatever differences they see in cyclical dynamics (e.g. the trajectories mapping out different domains in the state space) is representing something related to sensory processing and decision making that doesn't seem to have anything directly to do with peripheral motor neuron activity. In that sense it seems distinct from whatever M1 and premotor cortex are doing, even if M1 and premotor cortex also do some kind of sensory processing (e.g. proprioceptive) for feedback control.

However, the shift among regions of the state space do seem to have some parallels with motor activity as described by Gallego, et al. (2017) Neuron. where preparatory activity moves through a 'null space' that does not induce motion, whereas activity coincident with motor action shifts to a different domain of the state space that does induce action. That seems similar to what is shown here with trajectories transitioning from one domain of the state space during choices that depend on stimulus motion vs. choices that depend on stimulus color.

items.title: https://academic.oup.com/cercor/advance-article/doi/10.1093/cercor/bhab488/6524015
items.abstract: Skill learning induces changes in estimates of gray matter volume (GMV) in the human brain, commonly detectable with magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Rapid changes in GMV estimates while executing tasks may however confound between- and within-subject differences. Fluctuations in arterial blood flow are proposed to underlie this apparent task-related tissue plasticity. To test this hypothesis, we acquired multiple repetitions of structural T1-weighted and functional blood-oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) MRI measurements from 51 subjects performing a finger-tapping task (FTT; á 2 min) repeatedly for 30-60 min. Estimated GMV was decreased in motor regions during FTT compared with rest. Motor-related BOLD signal changes did not overlap nor correlate with GMV changes. Nearly simultaneous BOLD signals cannot fully explain task-induced changes in T1-weighted images. These sensitive and behavior-related GMV changes pose serious questions to reproducibility across studies, and morphological investigations during skill learning can also open new avenues on how to study rapid brain plasticity.

Interesting preprint about the mechanisms underlying the effect of less sharing of misinformation following accuracy prompts. @member
https://psyarxiv.com/kf8md/
items.title: Thinking more or thinking differently? Using drift-diffusion modeling to illuminate why accuracy prompts decrease misinformation sharing
items.abstract: Recent experiments have found that prompting people to think about accuracy reduces the sharing of misinformation. The cognitive mechanism that produces this effect, however, remains unclear. Do accuracy prompts cause people to "stop and think," increasing deliberation? Or do they change what people think about, drawing attention to accuracy? Since these two accounts predict the same behavioral outcomes (i.e., increased sharing discernment following a prompt), we used computational modeling of sharing decisions with response time data, as well as out-of-sample ratings of headline perceived accuracy, to test the accounts' divergent predictions across six studies (N = 5633). The results suggest that accuracy prompts do not increase the amount of deliberation people engage in. Instead, they increase the weight participants put on accuracy while deliberating. Our findings highlight the importance of understanding how social media distracts people from considering accuracy, and provide evidence for scalable interventions that redirect people's attention.
items.summary: Using drift-diffusion modeling of sharing decisions and response times across six studies, the authors found that accuracy prompts reduce misinformation sharing by increasing the weight given to accuracy rather than increasing overall deliberation.
items.key_finding: Accuracy prompts increased the weight placed on accuracy during deliberation without increasing deliberation time, as shown by drift-diffusion modeling across six studies (N=5633).

classification.notes: No neuroimaging; purely behavioral/computational modeling study, included as tangential to CANlab's computational modeling interests.

<!channel> @member reminded me of a few more RECENT summaries /meta-analyses of brain changes (or not) in chronic pain and the effect of treatment:

https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamanetworkopen/fullarticle/2774581 (no consistent differences in brain activation to evoked pain between people with and without chronic pain)

https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0149763421003560#sec0020 (brain changes in the context of pain and suffering - some of their brain labelling is not the most exact, but a comprehensive account of what might matter more vs. less in chronic pain)

https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fnins.2021.684926/full (trying to make sense of treatment effects on the brain of chronic pain patients - I like referring to that massive table for a quick overview - and am very thankful someone made the effort to summarize it like this)

comments.text:
I've gone over the third study. It's curious to me that all of the areas that are mentioned suggest abnormalities in ascending nociceptive input which is contrary to what I saw in the behavioral and imaging data when working with patients transitioning to chronic pain, and inconsistent with the lack of long term efficacy of peripheral interventions.

It's notable that they "limited the meta-analysis to fMRI results measured during painful tasks," so it's not actually a meta-analysis of chronic pain, it's a meta-analysis of evoked pain in chronic pain patients. The authors reveal an a priori bias towards sensory systems in the next few sentences writing, "We assumed that changes of affected functional and metabolic activities are driven by reduced pain intensity and unpleasantness in chronic pain patients."

They also mix a number of neuropathic and idiopathic conditions together: "Chronic pain conditions included FM (_n_ = 15), neuropathic pain (post-stroke central pain, post-herpetic neuralgia, CRPS, cervical spondylosis neck pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, and amputation/phantom limb pain; _n_ = 10), chronic low back pain (_n_ = 9), headache/migraine (_n_ = 8), chronic OA (knee or hand), IBS (_n_ = 7), chronic musculoskeletal pain, somatoform pain disorder, Crohn's disease, inflammatory bowel disease, erythromelalgia, and failed back surgery syndrome (_n_ = 1)"

The entire study seems to be entertaining an outdated perspective that fails to take into account a decade of work indicating important etiological differences across chronic pain conditions, contributions to chronic pain etiology from non-sensory factors, and the limitations of evoked phasic pain as a model for persistent pain. Maybe the latter is inevitable for a meta-analysis:  you can only meta-analyze old studies, so paradigms are necessarily going to be outdated, but the failure to distinguish among conditions is disappointing. I would have put phantom limb, neuropathic, OA pain and tendonitis into one category. These are conditions with either indisputable peripheral causes, high success rates of peripheral interventions, or both. Another category would have included chronic low back pain and chronic musculoskeletal pain, possibly with headache/migraine. These are conditions that often don't have obvious peripheral contributions, and fail to respond to peripheral interventions. I'm not sure about the rest. Either included them with the chronic back pain category or make a third category perhaps organized around prospective neuro-inflammatory conditions. I'd have kept post-stroke pain entirely in its own category, because it's the only condition I've ever seen where peripheral nociception is not necessary at all. Not to mention there are brain lesions involved which confound meta-analysis. The authors recognize some of these issues in the discussion, but it comes across like something added during the review process, because they o nothing about it even though divisions could have been done post-hoc after the main analysis.

The inclusion of both fMRI and PET data is nice though.
yeh, definitely not complete, but a useful summary of treatment effects on (some) brain measures at least. Any other metas/summaries of treatment effects you know and could post here?
I didn't read the paper, I use the Tables as a resource, thanks for reading it!

Ya, I don't know how I feel about people just dumping articles into the articles channel that they haven't read. For my part I dont post anything unless I've read it, and am willing to recommend it or otherwise think it deserves attention. I also tend to include a short summary explaining who should care and why. I dislike the low standards for article sharing here, but as far as I can tell I'm alone on that count.

@member you grouch. Though I do agree I enjoy getting ppl’s comments on the articles they share (“who should care and why”) @member thanks for sharing! I will dig in at some point soon. Though its not always clear to me how to interpret the meta-analysis results
@member omg, relax! I also tagged Carmen because these summaries are particularly useful to her. Yes, you are alone in your grumpiness.
plus, there is a one sentence summary   (or, what I found useful) associated with each linked I shared.
*sigh*

items.title: Effects of Chronic Pain Treatment on Altered Functional and Metabolic Activities in the Brain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Functional Neuroimaging Studies
items.abstract: Previous studies have identified altered brain changes in chronic pain patients, however, it remains unclear whether these changes are reversible. We summarized the neural and molecular changes in patients with chronic pain and employed a meta-analysis approach to quantify the changes. We included 75 studies and 11 of these 75 studies were included in the activation likelihood estimation (ALE) analysis. In the 62 functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies, the primary somatosensory and motor cortex (SI and MI), thalamus, insula, and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) showed significantly decreased activity after the treatments compared to baseline. In the 13 positron emission tomography (PET) studies, the SI, MI, thalamus, and insula showed significantly increased glucose uptake, blood flow, and opioid-receptor binding potentials after the treatments compared to baseline. A meta-analysis of fMRI studies in patients with chronic pain, during pain-related tasks, showed a significant deactivation likelihood cluster in the left medial posterior thalamus. Further studies are warranted to understand brain reorganization in patients with chronic pain compared to the normal state, in terms of its relationship with symptom reduction and baseline conditions.
items.summary: A systematic review and ALE meta-analysis of 75 fMRI and PET studies examined brain changes in chronic pain patients following treatment.
items.key_finding: Chronic pain treatment was associated with decreased fMRI activity but increased PET glucose uptake/blood flow in SI, MI, thalamus, and insula, with a significant deactivation cluster in the left medial posterior thalamus.
